The future slate of Resident Evil games will only continue to become more fascinating with each new release and announcement. For instance, Resident Evil 10 will be an enormous milestone for the franchise and could possibly feature the return of S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team’s Jill Valentine, and which mainline entry is chosen to be remade after Resident Evil Veronica may be quite telling.

There are Resident Evil remake rumors floating about with regard to virtually every game that hasn’t yet been remade, to be fair, but one could be more intriguing than the rest. Indeed, anyone who is a massive fan of Resident Evil 5 may not want to hold their breath. It could be a long but satisfying road to Capcom finally succumbing and exploring co-op gameplay again, and it may take a highly anticipated detour to a duology that fans are itching to revisit.

According to Dusk Golem, as per Twitter/X, “the possibility of doing a Rev 1 Remake has been tossed around.” Again, there are few Resident Evil games that haven’t had their names thrown around with the rumor or potential for them to one day receive a remake of their own, and it was only a matter of time until a sliver of credence was leant toward the belief that Resident Evil Revelations would be treated to one. Plus, if Resident Evil Revelations gets a remake, it’s almost guaranteed that its sequel will, too.

Fans seem to be generally excited about Resident Evil Revelations possibly receiving a remake, though user AKA_Sparda is skeptical about how bloated Capcom’s release schedule might be thereafter. Moreover, user Vagabond85 argues that they’d be pleased to see a Resident Evil Revelations remake make some tonal changes, writing, “The hypersexualization of characters like Jessica really kill the tone of an otherwise pretty strong entry.” However, remakes of Resident Evil Revelations and Resident Evil Revelations 2 would be thrilling due to where they land canonically and chronologically in the series.

Before Resident Evil Veronica was officially announced as a remake of Resident Evil Code: Veronica, it seemed unlikely that we’d ever get one. Resident Evil Code: Veronica is set between Resident Evil 3: Nemesis and Resident Evil 4, for instance, and thus, Resident Evil Veronica is launching out of order. This essentially means that any random Resident Evil game could get a remake and simply be sewn into the fabric of the remake timeline that’s been woven, but a Resident Evil Revelations remake would give much-needed context for the franchise’s most epic rivalry.

Ironically, Resident Evil Revelations is set before Resident Evil 5, after the events of Resident Evil Code: Veronica. And, because Resident Evil’s Chris Redfield appears in Code: Veronica, Revelations, and Resident Evil 5, a remake trilogy dedicated to Chris may be in store. Resident Evil Revelations and Revelations 2 are fairly distinct gameplay-wise, and their stories are incredibly unique with pieces of narrative and lore that are barely even remarked on in other mainline Resident Evil installments, so having them remade and repackaged for a new generation of players would be terrific.

#3400. Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

“I’m not one of those people that try to act like I don’t want the thing. I want the thing. I’m excited about the thing,” said recent Academy Award nominee Danielle Brooks. “I know how much it has impacted little Dani when I’ve watched Oprah Winfrey or Whoopi Goldberg or Viola Davis or Halle Berry receive [Oscars], and listened even to the speeches now, [from Emmy winners] Niecy Nash-Betts and Sheryl Lee Ralph. They push you to continue to work hard.”

Though her 2023 role in “The Color Purple” cemented the Grammy winner’s status as a performer who has at the very least been nominated for each letter of EGOT, the real reward the recognition among her peers has brought is the opportunity to executive produce and star in projects like the Walter Thompson-Hernandez film “If I Go Will They Miss Me,” which premiered at Sundance 2026 to rave reviews. “Yes, I have the desire to be receiving awards one day,” said Brooks, “but at the end of the day, I get to do that with my work. I get to do that with stories like ‘If I Go,’ where my goal is for people to feel seen.” Related Stories How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The coming-of-age drama set in Watts, California sees the actress play a mother named Lozita doing her best to hold her family together while there’s inscrutable tension between her partner, recently released from prison, and their imaginative 12-year-old son. “I started out in theater, so to me, it’s never been about a paycheck,” joked Brooks. “It’s always been about the story and what you’re putting out into the world. And so, when I watched [Thompson-Hernandez’s] short, I was like, ‘Yo, this is different. I ain’t never seen nothing like this.’ And it was captivating just the way he was shooting it.”

Expanding on what drew her to the project, which came to her during her time bouncing between Los Angeles awards press for “The Color Purple,” and the New Zealand set of “A Minecraft Movie,” Brooks said “They handed me the script and it was really the conversation, sitting down with Walter, his passion for his community, hearing about the real Lozita who had unfortunately passed away from cancer two years prior, hearing about the Compton Cowboys, just getting to talk to him about relationships between kids and their parents and the complications that it can bring.”

She said, “I like the balance. I got to have a little comedy, but I got to do some drama and it does my heart well.” While “Minecraft” brought her “laughs all day with Jack Black and Jason Momoa,” “If I Go” brought Brooks “purpose.” “I’m excited that we get to share stories like this where people are really dealing with their personal issues and healing and all of that stuff,” she said.

Having screened the film in Los Angeles the night before, Brooks said “You can feel the energy of everyone feeling super represented and feeling a sense of ownership. It’s cool hearing the audience be like, ‘Yeah, yeah,’ When you talk about the planes passing by, or the story about the fuel engines falling on elementary schools. People remember and know that to be a part of what has happened in LA, and the fabric of LA.”

One job that was foundational to how she approaches projects like “If I Go” happens to be Brooks’ breakout role as Taystee on “Orange Is the New Black.” Coming out of the prestigious Julliard School, her mind was more so on “how am I going to make my money for the subway and pay for my college tuition and how am I going to pay for this PB&J sandwich?,” when she booked the role on the series for the then-nascent streaming service Netflix. “I didn’t know what I was stepping into at the time. ‘Orange’ was looked at as a webseries, so nobody knew what this was about to be. But once we got into the work, I was like, ‘Oh, this is deeper than that.’ I remember talking to people who’ve been incarcerated, and I remember even doing a clothing drive for women who have just come out of prison so that they could have clothes for job interviews and stuff like that. We were really invested in the community and giving back,” said Brooks.

“We had that as a group, as storytellers, but then individually, I was watching my co-stars have a point of view, have something to say. And so, I [was] just learning that being an artist is also a form of activism,” she said. “That was one of the beginning seeds planted in my head once I was in the industry, because I’ve always known that what we do is about service, that’s number one. But I hadn’t experienced that on this level.”

Since then, Brooks’ goal has been to tell at least one story a year that incorporates a bit of activism, and with “If I Go,” the actress and producer has been more active than ever. “I’ve deemed us the little engine that could, because I really believe that we can take this far. My goal is that we just get as many eyeballs on it as we can. But the truth of the matter is nothing moves like money does. And that’s what I’ve learned is you’ve got to get really creative and strategic about how you can push a movie into the face of the people when you don’t have the money.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me,” distributed by Rich Spirit, has truly been an indie success story, making over $1 million at the box office from the humblest of beginnings. As Brooks noted, that haul has been hard fought, with her, Thompson-Hernandez, and her co-star J. Alphonse Nicholson touring as much of the country as they can to screen the film, and even abroad. “I’m going to Africa this week, I got invited, but then I learned there’s a film festival in Africa. So, I’m like, ‘Can we take the film to Africa?’ And they said, ‘Yes.’ So now, the film’s going to be in the festival there,” said the actress.

She continued, “It’s even in the form of fashion. People pay attention to what you’re wearing and then they’re like, ‘Why you got that on? Oh! She had a premiere.’ Boom. It’s insane how many tricks I have been working to get people to pay attention to this film that is worth paying attention to.”

One of the more beautiful aspects of this “If I Go” experience has been the way in which her community has shown up for her and the film. Snoop Dogg and Ava DuVernay have Instagrammed about it, while Helen Hunt and André Holland have even hosted talk backs for the film. But in terms of creativity, one marketing strategy takes the cake. “Issa Rae, even at her restaurant, she did a menu dedicated to ‘If I Go’ where it was a discount, 15 percent off or something if you bought a ticket,” she said. “People understand the importance of this,” said Brooks. “If the film wasn’t good, I wouldn’t be doing all this.”

On the awards front, the challenge is still getting the film in front of the steak eaters who still make up a good chunk of the awards body, and maybe do not immediately think they identify with the material. “The Academy is working really hard to change that narrative by who is allowed to vote. The voting party is shifting, but that’s what I’m experiencing right now,” said Brooks.

But regular filmgoers have a role in getting smaller, truly independent films awards recognition too. “The general audience plays a huge part because the culture tells the voters where to look, what is important,” said the actress. “The people, we have a voice in this too. I think we make it very clear what we want to see, but it’s a weird cycle.” Studio films have a budget for billboards, commercials, advertisements, and more. “When you are a small independent film, you have to be that big machine on your own to get it out there. And that’s a lot of work, and that’s a lot of time, and that’s a lot of smarts,” said Brooks. “You’ve got to have a lot of faith and hope too. You’ve just got to believe that what you’ve created is strong. And I do know that we all do, myself, J. Alphonse, Walter, MACRO, Rich Spirit, we believe in this film wholeheartedly.”

“Movies like these are worth telling, and I think they do reach who they need to reach, and they do lock in with the world on a larger scale when they’re supposed to,” said Brooks, reflecting on the fruitful journey “If I Go” has already had so far. “This is the thing I’m most proud of in my whole career because just the fact that people are having conversations, hard conversations with their loved ones, and they’re finding ways to heal.”

“If I Go Will They Miss Me” is now available to rent on all platforms.

#3399. As Apple works on AI agent features, banks are already blocking them

One of the most dramatic shifts in the AI landscape is the emergence of intelligent agents that can use iPhone and Mac apps in order to carry out tasks on our behalf.

We can already use third-party chatbots in this way, and we know Apple is working hard to turn Siri AI into an agent. However, before the company even gets the chance, banks are already blocking them, and this may be just the start …

The science fiction promise of AI has always been to be able to tell a computer what we want done and have the task carried out for us automatically. That’s starting to turn into a reality with the emergence of AI agents.

We’ve already seen Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, and Muse gain agent capabilities, and Apple is expected to bring these to Siri AI at some point next year.

Earlier this month, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said that the company ultimately wants to go in this direction and may add these abilities next year. CEO John Ternus has reportedly been pushing Craig Federighi for faster software development, with specific mention of “moving beyond necessary improvements to Siri,” which seems likely to mean agentic capabilities.

Last week also saw a since-deleted Apple job listing detailing plans for autonomous AI agents.

We’ve already seen some of the ways in which this can go wrong, and we recently outlined three significant risks. Wired reports that banks are now responding to these by either blocking AI agents or warning customers that using them can be dangerous.

JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

Wells Fargo even goes as far as using capitals in its latest terms, stating that it will not be responsible for the consequences.

Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK

We can likely expect similar pushback in sectors like online shopping as companies fear high returns costs and other consequences from mistakes by AI agents.

Personally, I don’t give any AI agents access to any of my banking or other financial services, considering the risks to be too high. I don’t see my position changing any time soon.

What’s your take? Would you trust an AI agent with access to your bank accounts? If not, would Apple launching agentic capabilities for Siri AI change your view? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3398. 7 Western Movies We Actually Want to See a Remake Of

The Western is easily one of cinema’s most iconic genres, having given us some of the greatest, most influential films of all time. As the genre’s popularity has waxed and waned over the decades, many of these influential films have been remade for a new generation of audiences, sometimes successfully and other times not. However, while remakes as a trend are generally seen in a negative light, some classic Westerns really could do with a modern remake.

Some Westerns are worth remaking because they’re timeless stories on the level of classical texts by this point, the cinematic equivalents of Shakespeare or The Odyssey. Others sorely need some retooling to fix the dated and derogatory depictions of communities that mar an otherwise exceptional work of art. Without further ado, here’s a look at some of the Western movies that we actually want to see a remake of, including some of the most notable films ever made in the genre.

Written and directed by John Huston, The Treasure of the Sierra Madre is a classic neo-Western adapted from B. Traven's 1927 novel. Humphrey Bogart and Tim Holt star as two down-on-their-luck men who join a grizzled old prospector (played by Huston’s father, Walter Huston) to search for gold in the titular mountain range. The movie also features Bruce Bennett, Barton MacLane, Alfonso Bedoya, and more in supporting roles.

Back in 1948, The Treasure of the Sierra Madre was a major critical and commercial hit, winning three Academy Awards, a BAFTA, and a Golden Globe. It’s still regarded as one of the greatest films of all time and a true masterpiece of the Western genre. As a practically canonical work of cinema, the movie is a landmark that’s certainly worth revisiting with modern actors and talent. Its core themes and narratives are timeless enough that the story would be just as impactful today as it was all those years ago.

Directed by John Ford and adapted from Dorothy M. Johnson’s 1953 short story, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance is notable for being the first time John Wayne and James Stewart starred in a movie together. The film is centered on Ransom "Ranse" Stoddard (Stewart), a young lawyer who’s beaten and robbed by the outlaw Liberty Valance but is saved by rancher Tom Doniphon (Wayne). What follows is a tale of friendship, love, and honor, with Vera Miles, Lee Marvin, John Carradine, and more in supporting roles.

A landmark Western that balances action, romance, politics, and drama with a surprisingly profound moral story, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance was popular with critics and audiences alike, becoming the 15th-highest-grossing film of 1962. Anchored by the performances of its evenly matched stars, the movie has had a significant impact on the genre and was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the Library of Congress. While its original story is firmly rooted in its time, its themes of political myth-making and moral arguments are still quite relevant today and worth revisiting.

A 1993 Western directed by George P. Cosmatos and written by Kevin Jarre, Tombstone is loosely inspired by real events from the 1880s, particularly the infamous Gunfight at the O.K. Corral and the Earp Vendetta Ride. Kurt Russell and Val Kilmer lead an ensemble cast as real-life lawmen Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday, with Sam Elliott, Bill Paxton, Powers Boothe, Michael Biehn, Dana Delany, and Charlton Heston in key supporting roles.

A star-studded, larger-than-life movie featuring some of the most notable real-life heroes and villains of the Wild West, Tombstone is the Western equivalent of The Avengers or, perhaps more accurately, The Expendables. It’s a highly entertaining film that was a critical and financial success in its day, and the movie is now regarded as a cult classic. Considering it’s been over three decades since it came out, a remake of Tombstone could help reintroduce a new generation of Western fans to its legendary characters and story.

Four icons and four completely different ways of walking into trouble. This is the one you would have been out there, why it fits, and what it would have cost you.

You have never explained yourself and you have never needed to, because people work out fairly quickly that you are the most capable person in the room without you ever having to mention it.

You are the funniest person in most rooms and the most loyal person in all of them, and you would be genuinely insulted if somebody suggested those two things were in any tension.

You never wanted this job, and you took it anyway because the alternative was standing there watching somebody less careful do it badly, which is the most Western reason there has ever been.

Nobody has ever successfully talked you out of something you had already decided was right, and a long line of grown adults has found that out the hard way.

A British Western directed by Burt Kennedy, Hannie Caulder was a rare movie for its time in that it features a woman in the role of lead gunfighter. Raquel Welch stars as the titular character, a frontier wife who runs a remote horse station with her husband. After a gang of criminals kills her husband, rapes her, and leaves her for dead, Hannie recruits a bounty hunter to help her get revenge by teaching her how to be a gunfighter.

Despite being wholly unlike any other movie in its genre at the time, Hannie Caulder performed quite well at the box office back in 1971. The film has sadly become more or less forgotten these days, which is why it could use a modern remake, but it has proven quite influential among genre filmmakers, with Quentin Tarantino in particular naming it as an influence on his work. Alongside its 1950s predecessor, Johnny Guitar, Hannie Caulder is one of the movies that helped pave the way for later female-led Westerns, though the two movies go about this in very different ways.

Directed by Don Siegel, Two Mules for Sister Sara is an American-Mexican co-production set in Mexico shortly after the American Civil War and during the Second Franco-Mexican War. Clint Eastwood stars as an American mercenary who meets a nun (Shirley MacLaine) and ends up helping her and her rebel allies in a risky operation against the French army. Besides Eastwood and MacLaine, the movie also stars Manolo Fábregas, Alberto Morin, David Estuardo, and more in supporting roles.

Two Mules for Sister Sara is a classic Clint Eastwood Western that arguably improves on the familiar formula by adding a screwball romance to the mix. The result is a movie that’s highly entertaining and masterfully crafted, with strong performances and direction. Though it was fairly well-received back in the '70s, the film isn’t as widely known these days, and it could definitely use a modern remake to reintroduce the rollicking story to a new generation of viewers.

Sidney Poitier’s directorial debut, Buck and the Preacher, is a revisionist Western that Poitier directed and starred in. Set shortly after the Civil War, the film follows Buck (Poitier) and his wife Ruth (Ruby Dee) as they lead wagon trains of African Americans from Louisiana to Kansas, fighting back against white raiders hired to harass them with the help of a mysterious individual who claims to be a preacher (Harry Belafonte). The movie also features Cameron Mitchell, Denny Miller, Nita Talbot, and more in supporting roles.

Long before movies like The Harder They Fall and Django Unchained, Buck and the Preacher broke ground as the first notable Western to feature a primarily Black cast. Though it’s not very widely known these days, the movie is both historically significant and highly entertaining. A remake of the classic makes a lot of sense, as the themes and story are certainly still resonant today, and it could also polish up some of the original movie’s flaws in pacing, particularly in its later half.

Directed by John Ford and adapted from Ernest Haycox’s 1937 short story The Stage to Lordsburg, Stagecoach is arguably the most iconic Western of Hollywood’s Golden Age. As the title suggests, the film is set on a stagecoach, exploring the stories of its passengers and the various dangers they encounter as they travel between Arizona and New Mexico. The movie stars John Wayne in his breakout role, leading an ensemble cast that also includes Claire Trevor, Andy Devine, John Carradine, Thomas Mitchell, and Louise Platt.

While the historical and cultural significance of Stagecoach cannot be denied, the film’s representation of Native Americans is highly derogatory and dated, which is one of the biggest reasons to give it a modern remake. The movie already had a remake back in 1966, which was similarly acclaimed and similarly problematic by modern standards, and another one in 1986, which was less problematic but also less acclaimed, so this is one Western classic that could really do with another try, even if it is an undeniable cultural landmark as is.

#3395. 16-Episode Existential Sci-Fi Masterpiece On Netflix Is A God-Tier Adaptation

Some sci-fi stories are so profoundly human, introspective, and existential on the page that adapting them on the screen should be impossible. More often than not, even some of the most ambitious filmmakers leave such stories alone. However, every once in a while, someone dares to translate such stories to the screen and the result turns out to be beyond impressive.

Perhaps Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival is an incredible example of this. The sci-fi movie turns Ted Chiang's stories into a masterful exploration of time, destiny, free will, and the stories we tell ourselves to find meaning. Similar to Arrival, the sci-fi series, Pantheon, goes to extreme lengths to capture the essence of Ken Liu's award-winning sci-fi stories.

Like Denis Villeneuve’s Arrival, Pantheon seems fairly simple in its early moments. The sci-fi show on Netflix unfolds in a world where mind-uploading technology is becoming accessible for the masses. However, what starts as a tale about a global conspiracy evolves to an existential scale that questions everything from humanity's place in the universe to the nature of consciousness.

Ted Chiang's novella, Story of Your Life, was seemingly never meant to be adapted for the screen. It heavily relies on teleological physics and linguistic relativity to explore time travel. Yet, screenwriter Eric Heisserer and director Denis Villeneuve turned it into a 2-hour cinematic masterpiece by tricking viewers into reading flash-forwards as flashbacks.

In Pantheon, creator Craig Silverstein picks up many of Ken Liu's short stories that present fragmented explorations of post-humanity. He then binds them into a singular narrative that starts a relatable family drama but grows into an existential war story. Pantheon does not shy away from being incredibly ambitious with its storytelling. But, like Denis Villeneuve's Arrival, it never forgets it is about its human characters.

On the screen, science fiction can risk feeling too sterile and hollow if its ambition outgrows its human stakes. There are cosmic elements in both Arrival and Pantheon that give a glimpse of how insignificant human lives can seem in the vastness of the universe. Yet, in both, the high-concept sci-fi is always anchored in human grief.

Pantheon originally premiered on AMC+, but it is now available for streaming on Netflix in the U.S.

Arrival introduces an alien language through ink-ring logograms to make sense out of an abstract concept like non-linear time. It never dumbs this down and respects viewers' intelligence by allowing them to do a lot of intellectual heavy lifting. Pantheon achieves something similar by using animating as a visual language as it walks through complex ideas surrounding

In the best existential sci-fi books, post-humanity is the threshold. They question whether a machine can think or whether achieving singularity would be a boon or bane for humanity. Pantheon, in contrast, blows right past this. Boom! The series keeps pushing the boundaries of existential sci-fi until it is far beyond base realities, linear time, and biological life.

It begins with a familiar exploration of how digital cloning and consciousness uploading can pave the way for many moral and ethical challenges. Once uploading becomes safe, it shifts to a civilizational schism, showing how those who refuse to "upload" themselves are biological relics while the ones who conformed are almost godlike.

Before its credits start rolling, Pantheon also ambitiously leaps millions of years ahead in time. With this, it attempts to highlight how, despite becoming almost godly omnipresent beings with the ability to simulate infinity, meaning only exists in human vulnerability and the inability to know what lies ahead. Here lies the beauty of Pantheon's unforgettable exploration of existential sci-fi.

#3394. ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down

[Editor’s Note: The following review contains spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 Episode 8, “The Tower” — including the finale’s ending.]

“I saw the structure of the episode as these kind of waves that crash upon Lee,” Ethan Hawke said in an interview about “The Lowdown‘s” Season 2 finale. “The way life works, it’s not like, ‘Oh, this one thing happens and then you change.’ It’s usually a series of things that happen, and the walls of your defenses come down.”

Lee’s walls were certainly up when “The Lowdown” Season 2 began. Untethered by the acclaim for his Season 1 exposé on Dale Washberg (Tim Blake Nelson), Lee reacts with vehement defensiveness. He mocks the journalists who named him Tulsa’s Journalist of the Year during his acceptance speech. He alienates his friends and embarrasses his daughter. Related Stories Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’ Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

He’s a mess, and when Ginger (Betty Gilpin) walks into his life with a tantalizing new story, he’s lucky — not because she’s the woman of his dreams carrying his drug of choice (a “truthstorian’s” next crusade), but because grounding forces are on the way in the form of his estranged father, Lee Raybon Sr. (Tommy Lee Jones), as well as a few clear-eyed, full-throated friends. Over the course of a riveting, revelatory Season 2, they all help to bring Lee back to himself, one wave at a time.

The finale’s first swell comes as quite a surprise — two surprises, really. When Lee pulls up to the funeral home, prepared to pay a terse goodbye to his departed dad, so, too, does his former business partner and best friend, Wendell (played by Peter Dinklage). Wendell tells Lee he’ll “always be grateful” for Senior’s guidance when they were younger, and it’s immediately clear he’s not about to take the man’s final tribute as lightly as his son may have hoped.

“When Tommy’s character dies and there’s a funeral, we’re all like, ‘Well, wouldn’t Wendell be there?’ I mean, they’re really great friends,'” Hawke said. “I called Peter up and I was like, ‘Is there any way you’d come down for one day to be just at this funeral?’ And Peter was shooting in London and flew in and flew right back. He came in and made it happen for us.”

But Dinklage’s return was no mere cameo. Creator Sterlin Harjo knew better than to let the opportunity go to waste.

“I think there was a Shakespeare monologue in it first, and it was beautiful,” Harjo said. “Then Peter suggested the Dylan Thomas. […] I can’t imagine a more exciting way to have Peter be in your show than doing this Dylan Thomas poem that’s a gentle poem, but he does it with this rage — how it’s supposed to be read. It’s amazing.”

Volunteering to speak when Ray (Michael Hitchcock) gets overwhelmed, Wendell spends a few seconds scrolling to find the right poem (“Do not go gentle into that good night”) and then tears into it with vigor. Dinklage’s recitation is more of a resuscitation — powerful enough to wake the dead, it wakes Lee up, snapping him into the present and bringing him back to life.

“When he’s doing the poem, he came in at a 10,” Harjo said. “The only direction I gave him was, ‘What if you build to that?’ And that’s what he did, and it was just unbelievably great.”

“That one is violent and abrupt,” Hawke said. “It’s a friend shaking you up.”

In Hawke’s case, Lee’s friend was his real friend. He knew Dinklage “loved poetry,” and he even knew a little bit about what his fellow actor would bring to this poem.

“This is where collaboration is really mysterious about how it works and when it works really well,” Hawke said. “I’ve been friends with Peter Dinklage since, I don’t know, 1990. […] We both arrived in New York around the same time, and we used to sit around and tie one on and try to flirt with girls and read poems. We used to geek out about how much we loved the ways people would read poems in the old days. If you hear Dylan Thomas read a poem or you hear Orson Wells read a poem, they weren’t afraid of feeling or emotion or a theatricality. They weren’t afraid of passion — actual passion — and caring and looking foolish.”

“We’re living in an age of irony and cynicism and detachment, and this definition of cool being that you don’t care. Whereas the definition when I was growing up was Bob Marley and John Lennon and Miles Davis and those guys cared a tremendous amount. They weren’t detached. They were completely attached. So for me to watch Peter bring that to his performance was like, ‘Let me show you kids how to do a poem!’ [laughs] ‘You got to do it like your life depends on it.'”

“The key to that scene is the interaction between him and Lee,” Harjo said. “I love that he’s watching Lee the whole time. It’s like there’s no one else in the room and he’s doing it for Lee. I love that.”

“The camera does pick up subconscious,” Hawke said. “A lot of times I’ll see work that might be good, but it has no subconscious to it. I can tell there’s no secret sewn into the filmmaking. And Sterlin loves — you can call it poetry, you can call it whatever you want — but [he loves] when there’s multiple layers happening. […] And so for me, I’m not just sitting there with an actor doing this scene. I’ve known this guy for 30 years and I know what this poem means to him, and he knows me.”

“If there was an Academy Award for Best Single Scene, I would give it to Peter Dinklage in our show.”

While Dinklage may have to settle for an Emmy, Harjo had to write the other big finale monologue for an actual Oscar winner. At the reception, Lee’s daughter Francis (Ryan Kiera Armstrong) reads a passage from her grandfather’s journal, written shortly after Lee Jr. was born, as a way to honor her ancestor. Then, as Francis speaks Senior’s words, Senior appears seated behind her, and Tommy Lee Jones takes over the scene.

“The bigger thing about that monologue is I knew it was coming,” Harjo said. “I was like, ‘Oh shit, I got to write this thing for Tommy Lee Jones.’ I kind of had Tommy Lee Jones dialed in through the whole season. I felt like I could really write his voice. But when it came to that monologue, I’m like, ‘God, he’s already known for one of the best monologues in the world at the end of ‘No Country for Old Men,’ and I can either try to do a fancy monologue that isn’t like that at all, or I could lean into the fact that Cormac McCarthy and the Coen brothers did this really well already, and there’s no way that I don’t know that as a filmmaker. So I’m going to lean into it and almost give homage to that speech.'”

“Not to toot my own horn, but I feel like I nailed it,” he said, laughing. “Of course, it filters through Tommy Lee Jones and all of a sudden it’s like this fucking amazing thing that he does. It was wonderful being on set. Just watching him give that, it was unbelievable. I could have used any take and it would’ve been amazing in a different way.”

Throughout the monologue, Lee sits in thoughtful silence. He’s not only absorbing what his father wrote and remembering who he was; he’s also recognizing his shifting role as a son who’s now a father. There’s a connection across generations. Yes, his responsibility to his daughter means avoiding repeating his dad’s mistakes, which Lee is well-aware of, but it also means honoring his father’s better intentions, like the ones he voiced in that journal and Francis is voicing again now.

“Lee’s adamant that he’s nothing like his father,” Hawke said. “The first thought I had is, ‘All right, this is why Lee Raybon is obsessed with the truth: It’s that his father was a chronic liar.’ If you grew up in a house where your parent was really comfortable lying to you, you would get obsessed with people in power misleading you, and that would really drive you.”

“But then as we played the scenes deeper, I realized that Lee was lying to himself; that he was just as manipulative as his father is. He just does it in the name of truth. All this bad behavior that he was in denial of, he’d actually internalized it, and he was so much like his dad that he was completely blind to it, which is behavior I’ve seen in so many friends. It’s amazing. But I had to live through it. I didn’t get it when I was reading it. I got it when I was playing it, and that was very powerful for me.”

One way Harjo & co. illustrate Lee’s development over the course of Season 2 is simple: He listens. Instead of shouting, pontificating, or generally causing chaos, Lee spends much of the finale hearing what everyone around him has to say. Even when he’s up his own ass or annoying the hell out of folks, he has a community who cares about him, and their steady presence in his life is what eventually breaks down his defenses.

“The first [wave] is Peter reading that poem, and then the second one is gentle and persuasive where my daughter is revealing to me that my father did love me,” Hawke said. “Part of the thing you learn watching this show is that Lee feels like he has to conquer the world to be worthy of self-respect. His daughter is saying, ‘It’s right here for you, and it always has been.'”

While another monologue played a significant role in how the episode plays out — Ginger’s speech to Francis, outside the bookstore — that moment wasn’t about Lee. (“The whole idea was Ginger and Francis don’t really get to hang out, but they are alike,” Harjo said. “Ginger immediately recognizes it and probably also knows that she had a father that was a lot like Lee.”) So his final wave comes from a curious source.

“The third one is just this final little moment that happens with Vickey (Abbie Cobb) when she tells him his fortune is bad and he sees it as a good thing. He understands that everything is point of view, and for him, towers coming down would be good.”

“Those are the three steps that I think are designed to get Lee back on his feet again,” Hawke said. “That push him to be like, ‘All right, you know what? I’m not quitting. I’m going to keep being me, and I’m going to be a better version of me.'”

How he’s feeling when Season 3 starts is anyone’s guess, and that assumes a renewal that’s yet to be announced is still in the offing from FX. But one thing’s for sure: If Lee comes back, he’ll be a changed man — and he won’t be alone.

“The Lowdown” is available on FX and Hulu.

#3393. Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO of Nvidia, stock up 30%

Nvidia has announced that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The company’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so …

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

That changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the company’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

Money over country. This is government intervention.

Despite putting the company at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones said: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”

That changed today, with the company making the announcement in a press release.

Nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Company. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”

As previously announced, in light of recent reporting that Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, the Board formed a committee comprised solely of independent directors to investigate, and the committee retained independent counsel to assist it in that investigation. The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.

The company’s stock price jumped by more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also up per Yahoo Finance.

#3392. Apple's AirPods Pro 3 Are $100 Off During Black Friday

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are not only my favorite earbuds I've ever owned, they might also be my favorite headphones of all time. The Pros sound great, come with excellent noise cancellation and transparency modes, and are packed with modern features that go beyond listening to music. I'd recommend these to any Apple user looking for the best overall audio experience at full price, but when they're $100 off, I actively encourage you to buy these now.

On the surface, Apple's third-generation AirPods Pro are among the best ways to listen to audio on your Apple devices. The earbuds sound great: I'm not an audiophile or a headphone reviewer, but to my ears, the Pros deliver excellent sound quality, with plenty of bass and great sound separation. I frequently turn to mine when I want to pay close attention to a new album, or watch a show or movie with intricate sound design. Plus, like other AirPods, the Pros are great for jumping between your various Apple devices. I'm constantly switching between my iPhone, Mac, and Apple TV with mine, and they seamlessly move between each—at least, most of the time.

The noise cancellation on these AirPods is also stellar. I used to take my AirPods Max with me on planes, but lately, I've been fine with just my Pros, since the noise cancellation seemingly blocks just about as much background sound as my over-the-ear headphones. Equally great are both the transparency modes, which pump in outside sounds while you're wearing your AirPods, and Adaptive Transparency, which automatically adjusts the level of transparency based on how loud or soft your surroundings are. This is a great mode for wearing your AirPods in loud environments, so you can still hear everything without the noise becoming overwhelming. To that point, these AirPods are actually FDA-certified hearing aids.

There are plenty of other features available here as well, especially if you have a compatible iPhone. AirPods Pro 3 have a built-in heart rate sensor, so you can track workouts without an Apple Watch; you can translate conversations in real time with Live Translate; "Conversation Awareness" lowers the volume of your audio and turns on transparency mode when you start speaking; and they run for eight hours on one charge with noise cancellation enabled.

This isn't an in-depth list of the AirPods Pro 3's set of features. But suffice it to say, these earbuds are worth their full MSRP of $249. So not only can I wholeheartedly recommend them at $149, but I'd say they're an easy buy if you've been thinking about picking up AirPods for yourself.

#3391. Netflix's Near-Perfect 8-Episode Sci-Fi Series Is a Weekend Binge Worth Revisiting

Perhaps one of streaming's greatest tragedies was the shocking cancellation of the pitch-perfect sci-fi dark comedy The Boroughs. While the logistical reasons are certainly understandable, the series' brilliance may have thrown some viewers for a loop. The eight-episode Netflix series, created by Jeffrey Addiss and Will Matthews and executive produced by the Duffer Brothers, follows a grieving widower who relocates to a seemingly picturesque retirement community, only to discover something sinister lurking underneath. With a dynamic mix of cozy mystery elements and daring sci-fi tropes, The Boroughs moves across genre lines to deliver an emotional, character-driven story.

When Sam Cooper (Alfred Molina), a recently widowed retired aerospace engineer, moves into the idealistic New Mexico retirement community known as The Boroughs, he soon realizes that everything is not what it seems. After noticing mysterious deaths and unexplained disappearances that local authorities ignore, he discovers an ominous threat operating behind the scenes. Sam teams up with a misfit group of fellow residents to stop this otherworldly threat that is harvesting their time and life force.

Though the premise is rooted in sci-fi intrigue, what makes The Boroughs unique are the individuals at the center of the story. Like Stranger Things did with teenage sleuths, The Boroughs focuses on a generation often deemed "too old" to play in the sci-fi sandbox. As with stories like The Thursday Murder Club, unsuspecting underdogs make the most fascinating protagonists. They aren't presented as wise mentors who assist younger adventure-seekers but actually take the lead themselves, investigating the supernatural threats lurking beneath their seemingly idyllic community.

Netflix's inability to create sustained hits could result in long-term issues.

However, The Borough's eight episodes don't shy away from the elephant in the room, with the characters' ages playing a major role in the action. By diving deep into the realities of aging, including managing cancer medication, memory care concerns, and grief, the series presents their daring journey as something bigger than simply letting time get the best of them. When the characters do have moments to reflect and grapple with mortality, loneliness, and purpose, these themes are presented as universal realities that viewers of any age can relate to, emphasizing the brilliance of Addiss and Matthews' creation.

The Boroughs is a beautifully crafted series, with practical and technical worldbuilding playing an equally important part in the storytelling. The show was filmed across the great state of New Mexico, and its cul-de-sac was crafted to feel warm and welcoming, creating an immersive setting. Other parts of the community are imbued with nostalgia, giving the characters a reason to reminisce while also doubling as a means of emotional entrapment.

Visuals aside, The Boroughs taps some heavy hitters to play the story's senior-citizen sleuths. The acclaimed ensemble, featuring the likes of Molina, Geena Davis, Alfre Woodard, Bill Pullman, Clarke Peters, and Denis O'Hare, captures the genuine heart of the show. Molina is quite grounded as the standoffish and guarded Sam Cooper, while Davis gets to lean into the cougar trope, clearly having immense fun as Renee. Woodard and Peters earn the most complex and alluring relationship, and their moments of emotional intimacy are welcome amid the wild sci-fi chaos happening around them. O'Hare is at his finest, bringing nuance to an individual who knows the end is near. Perhaps the most heartbreaking performance comes from Ed Begley Jr. as Edward, a man who lives in The Manor, the long-term care wing.

Given the cast's terrific on-screen chemistry, any scene shared by these elite actors feels like a masterclass in acting. They're so strong that the prospect of more to the story was quite exciting until Netflix pulled the plug. Reported production costs of $10 million or more per episode, the high-caliber cast, and an alleged viewership drop-off were cited as factors in Netflix's decision to cancel The Boroughs after one season. Once you finish this near-perfect series, you'll be stunned that the business side of television got in the way of something truly special.

#3390. Star Trek: Duty And Honor Officially Brings Back Worf

Star Trek fans will almost certainly be familiar with the legendary character Worf. The Klingon, first introduced in Star Trek: The Next Generation, has appeared in more episodes throughout the entire show's history than any other character, making him both a fan-favorite staple and a constant fixture. It is for this very reason that his reappearance on multiple shows and subsequent new Star Trek content no longer feels terribly surprising, although it is always appreciated.

Fortunately, for those who cannot get enough of Worf and want a brand-new Star Trek release to tide them over, the iconic character is returning once more in a new release that is targeted at dedicated fans. Titled Duty and Honor, this new Star Trek project offers a different type of experience than the one most fans will be used to, all while putting Worf front and center. Suffice it to say, it could end up being the definitive Worf Star Trek release should its creators play their cards right.

Duty and Honor is the upcoming expansion for the critically acclaimed deck-building game, Star Trek: Captain's Chair. The base game, for those who've missed out thus far, is an in-depth, strategic experience in which players take on the role of one of six captains (either Picard, Sisko, Burnham, Shran, Koloth, and Sela) and must attempt to complete various objectives and obtain the highest score by playing cards from each character's corresponding starter deck and any they obtain throughout.

Widely praised as being a compelling and highly detailed Star Trek experience with strong theming and phenomenal representation of the characters included, Captain's Chair (developed by WizKids) has gone on to get multiple expansions. The latest, the aforementioned Duty and Honor, adds four new captains to the experience, as well as their corresponding decks, thus greatly increasing the level of replayability and variety within the game.

Duty and Honor is adding Captain Worf as well as the fan-favorite Deep Space Nine Cardassian, Gul Dukat. Two additional captains will also be added, although WizKids has not yet confirmed who they will be. Of course, included in their decks will be iconic ships, characters, and locations associated with them, so dedicated fans are in for a treat. While it isn't quite a new series, it should hopefully make up for the canceled Worf series that fans never got the chance to see.

The base Star Trek: Captain's Chair game that is required to play the Duty and Honor expansion costs $59.99. It is currently available for back-order on the official WizKids website and is expected to be shipped in Q4 2026.

The Duty and Honor expansion for Star Trek: Captain's Chair costs $39.99. It is currently available for pre-order via the official WizKids website, as well as other assorted retailers. It is estimated to have a release date of Q3 2027, according to the official store listing, which means it'll release any time between July 1 and September 30. Considering how well-received the other Star Trek: Captain's Chair expansions have been, fans can likely rest assured that Duty and Honor will do Worf proud.

#3389. Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published on April 24, 2026, when “I Swear” was released in American theaters. Aramayo recently won Best Actor in a Film at the BAFTA Scotland Awards. The film and his performance are eligible for this year’s Oscars, and “I Swear” is now streaming on Netflix.]

When Robert Aramayo signed on to play Scottish Tourette’s activist John Davidson in filmmaker Kirk Jones’ biopic “I Swear,” he could scarcely imagine where the film would take him.

A hit in the UK, the film netted Aramayo a pair of BAFTA wins earlier in the year, as the British actor won both the vaunted Rising Star Award (previous winners include James McAvoy, John Boyega, Tom Holland, Tom Hardy, and those are just some of its biggest names) and the Best Actor trophy (beating out Timothée Chalamet, Leonardo DiCaprio, Ethan Hawke, Jesse Plemons, and eventual Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan). Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

But that’s hardly all that happened at the February awards show, which was instantly and forever marred by a number of loud, racist outbursts from Davidson himself that were directed at “Sinners” stars Jordan, Delroy Lindo, Wunmi Mosaku, and more. The fallout from the incident was both swift and prolonged, and will likely impact the domestic release of “I Swear,” which is rolling out in stateside theaters now.

Aramayo’s performance in the film is indeed star-making and awards-worthy, as he brings sensitivity and great courage to his portrayal of Davidson, following him from his earliest symptoms through his current passionate activism. Hopefully, viewers can see and appreciate the work on its own merits, and get to know Aramayo much better, though he has previously appeared in plenty of projects recognizable to American audiences, from “The Empty Man” to “The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” to a little thing called “Game of Thrones” (young Ned Stark!).

Ahead, Aramayo tells IndieWire about his deep research for the role, everything BAFTAs, and what he hopes will come from more people seeing the film and, hopefully, understanding Tourette’s all the better.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When I saw the film at TIFF in September, I did my due diligence before I reviewed it, and learned that John is a huge figure in the UK, but relatively unknown in America. How much did you know about him before this film?

Robert Aramayo: John’s made a lot of documentaries, but the big one that probably had the most impact was “John’s Not Mad,” and that was in 1989. So if you speak to people who were around then, they have a lot of very personal stories about watching that documentary and being like, “Wow, is this Tourette’s? What’s Tourette’s?”

So when you get the script, are you someone who then wants to do more research into him, or do you feel like the script is the thing?

The production team and Kirk were so gracious, and they gave me so much time. I think they were like, “Oh, yeah, take a couple of months or something to research and stuff.” I was really thankful for that. The first thing that I did was to meet John; I met him very quickly. And then I went away for a month, and I spent that time gaining as much knowledge as I could about Tourette’s and what it is. That was through watching the documentaries, watching YouTube videos, and reading books.

I based myself in Galashiels and spent weeks with John, just following him around and spending as much time with him as I could. And also traveling through Scotland, meeting people, mainly through [support organization] Tourette Scotland, who lived with Tourette’s as well. I wanted to have, I don’t know, a more expansive view of Tourette’s than just John. Obviously, John was my main focus, though.

When you’re getting ready to meet John, what were you expecting and anticipating? What were you nervous about?

I don’t know what I felt, really. I was so filled with anxiety about, oh my word, am I going to do this? I wanted John to like me. I was already feeling, God, this is going to be a really big challenge. And I met him within days of saying yes.

But then, when I met him, one thing that struck me straight away was his knowledge. He’s got a really amazing knowledge about, obviously, Tourette’s, but also a lot of neurodiversity and how it lives, other conditions that exist with Tourette’s, and stuff like that. He’s got a lot of thoughts about how we can do better and help young people and things like that. He’s very forthcoming with it.

He’s got so much heart. He’s such an amazing, welcoming, supportive man that I was just like, wow, this is a really impressive person that I’m meeting here. Of course, then your anxiety and the responsibility meter have gone through the roof.

Just watching the film, I learned so much about what Tourette’s can entail and the very wide spectrum of symptoms that people can have. What was the most unexpected thing you learned about it during your research?

A couple of things really that had a really big impact on me straight away, and that sort of broke my perception of what I thought Tourette’s was, that anything can be a tic, and that it’s so singular to the person. So if you’ve met one person with Tourette’s, someone said to me, you’ve met one person with Tourette’s. That was a big thing.

And also the fact that there’s a lot of tics that you just don’t see. There’s tics that you don’t see as tics because anything can be a tic, or there’s tics that exist only in somebody’s mind, and things like that, tics linked with OCD. Just the complexity of it was massive.

I learned some statistics recently, which I found really interesting: One in 50 kids in America live with persistent tic disorder, and one in 160 live with Tourette’s, so it’s unbelievably common, it’s everywhere. We have met people with Tourette’s, we meet them all the time. It was part of the experience of the film as well, we met loads of people who were living with Tourette’s undiagnosed. 50 percent of people who live with Tourette’s in the U.S. are undiagnosed, and that was true for us in the UK as well in our experience. Maybe the thing is that we don’t know that that’s what’s happening. That made me think, wow, there’s a real educational piece to this as well.

You are playing someone who is a real person who has been captured on film for many years. People know what he looks like, they know what he sounds like. How do you find the line between impersonation and impression in your performance?

I never wanted to impersonate John. I think I would’ve gone the wrong way if that was what I was thinking. You have to, at a certain point, take ownership of the character and try and make him your own. I was lucky because there was so much that I needed to learn, so for so long, I wasn’t thinking about performance or playing him at all. I was just trying to immerse myself as much as I could in everything, anything that I could get my hands on. Then, at certain point, I moved to thinking about how I was going to try and play my version of John.

In a [narrative] film, you get the opportunity to maybe show a little bit more [than a documentary]. A documentary film crew comes into somebody’s life and they can capture what they can capture, but we could capture way more intimate moments throughout the whole film that John had spoken to.

We could show the moments where he is on his own, whether there’s been an impact or how he’s feeling or his emotional life, how things change over time and stuff like that, and hopefully try and do it with truth and authenticity.

You attended Juilliard, which always seems a little, “Oooohhh, he’s Juilliard-trained.”

But now that you’re a few years out of school, what are the pieces of training that are proving to be most useful to you?

I think that acting teachers and drama school is vocabulary, really. At the time, certain things that teachers would say to me had a massive impact on me and really opened me up to other ways of looking at things, and other things are only impacting me now, as I keep working and as I get older. I think that’s the beauty of drama school, you get flooded with all of this stuff, and then you’re going, “Oh, that’s what they were talking about.” And then there’s things that my teachers would consistently say, “You’ve got to work on this, you’ve got to work on this,” and I’m still working on it. It’s like a toolbox, and every now and again you go, “Oh, yeah, that’s what I need.”

They also made us do liberal arts which — I’m from Yorkshire, I don’t even know what liberal arts meant — but I’d encounter Nietzsche and Plato and all this stuff. I had no time at all to digest anything, but I’d read it and be like, “I don’t really know what’s going on here, but I think this is going to be important one day. I think I’m going to reread this one day!”

What was the morning of the BAFTA nominations like for you?

I knew it was happening that morning. I remember talking to my agent, and we just didn’t speak about it, but we both knew that they were coming out that morning or whatever, so we had a really chill conversation about something else. [Laughs] I put it on in the background, because I thought we had a chance at, I don’t know, something, and then I heard that Peter had been nominated and I was so happy for him. I was elated for him.

So, I was just in that, and I was doing the dishes, and I was like, “Wow, that’s so cool. I can’t wait to go text him.” And then they said my name, and I just absolutely couldn’t believe it. My agent called me back straight away and was like, “Oh, my God.” It was an amazing feeling, but it was really unexpected because I was still really, really sort of overwhelmed by the Rising Star thing.

You genuinely looked so surprised when you won Best Actor at the show. I feel like I would black out in that moment. Do you remember what that moment felt like?

Yeah, because I almost did! I had this weird physical reaction where I sort of went back [pantomimes sitting way back], and I think somebody grabbed me. I think I would’ve just kept going. I would’ve fallen off my chair or something.

I honestly couldn’t believe it. I’m honestly not sure I still can believe that that’s something that happened to me, because for someone like me to be in that group of people blew my mind. I felt like, “Wow, and there I am, that’s my name.” To me, that was the thing that sort of really, really, really, really blew me away. When it happened, yes, it all just becomes a blur, and I’m running down the stairs, and I don’t know what the hell I’m going to say.

Obviously, other things happened at the awards show involving John. As someone who had seen the film, I felt like I had a greater grasp on what was happening; I had that context. Now that the film is coming out in America, what hopes do you have for people seeing the film and how that might impact that conversation?

I think lots of people watch the film, and they feel like their education around Tourette’s has improved and increased, and that would be amazing [if that continued]. I think it’s important to acknowledge that … Tourette’s has an impact on a person who’s ticcing, and the same tic obviously has an impact on the person who’s receiving the tic or impacted by the tic. And it’s important to acknowledge that, because that is what it is. Coprolalia, which is the tic that John has, that tic, it’s not saying what you think, it’s saying the worst thing imaginable. That’s how it was described to me.

I hope people watch the film. And I hope people watch the film and think, “Oh, I’ve learned something about Tourette’s.” I hope that people watch the film from the community, because that’s been an amazing thing as well. People watching it who have lived with Tourette’s or lived with another neurodiverse condition have reached out and said, “I see myself in this.” You want people to go to the movies and enjoy the film, but if people go home and Google “John Davidson” or Google “Tourette’s,” that’d be amazing.

The film is going to introduce you to a much larger audience, but you’ve also been in some massive hits before this one. Which is a fun way to ask: Do you know that “The Empty Man” has a huge cult fandom?

[Laughs] I’ve been told this. What an experience. I loved making that film. It was a long journey with it, and I learned a lot. And it was my first movie that I’d done with James Badge Dale, and I did another one with him as well. And I really, really liked working with him. He’s a really nice guy, and he’s a really talented actor. And the director, David [Prior], was wonderful. I learned a lot on that film. I love that people love that film.

You are also in the “Lord of the Rings” world as well. Are you going to be turning out to see “The Hunt for Gollum”?

I’m so excited. I can’t wait. I’m a massive fan of the Peter Jackson films. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. It’s a really interesting story. I’m glad that they’re doing it and doing it properly.

Now that you’ve had what feels like a big breakthrough, what sort of things are you pursuing next?

What do I want to do next? I don’t know! I feel lucky to just be an actor, to work. I’ve been lucky enough to work with some incredible people on “I Swear,” to work with Kirk and Peter and Shirley and Maxine. People like that, you learn, you grow, you get better. And so if I can just keep doing it, I’ll be happy.

That Rising Star Award feels like a lot of pressure!

I just feel really, really grateful for everyone who voted for me. It’s such a cool award that the public, the British public, vote for you. I feel so grateful for everyone who voted for me. I just feel very, very grateful for the whole thing, for everything, and mainly that people hopefully watch the film and talk about it.

For more information about Tourette Syndrome and access to free resources and support, visit the Tourette Association of America right here.

#3386. Reality Is Even Darker Than Jonathan Nolan & J.J. Abrams' 103-Episode Sci-Fi Masterpiece Predicted

Even though Jonathan Nolan and JJ Abrams’ underrated sci-fi series from the 2010s explored a dystopian vision of a surveillance state, reality ended up outdoing this CBS hit. When Firefly was canceled after only 14 episodes in 2002, there is no way that the show’s creators could have known just how influential the short-lived series would be. Without Firefly, viewers might never have gotten SyFy’s Dark Matter, Killjoys, or Bass X Machina, not to mention the show’s influence on the Guardians of the Galaxy movies.

Similarly, author Phillip K. Dick's contributions to the world of sci-fi literature had an almost immeasurable influence on the genre in the years after their original publication. His short story “We Can Remember It For You Wholesale” was loosely adapted into director Paul Verhoeven’s satirical sci-fi action thriller Total Recall, while his sci-fi noir novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? spawned the entire Blade Runner franchise.

Arriving on CBS in 2011, when Fringe’s success and the arrival of 2008’s theatrical spinoff The X-Files: I Want to Believe had reignited interest in sci-fi police procedurals, Person of Interest also benefitted from a killer premise. Person of Interest followed Jim Caviezel’s CIA officer John Reese as he began working with an eccentric inventor and billionaire tech mogul, Harold Finch.

Finch’s invention, simply called “The Machine,” was designed to use an algorithm to predict when terrorist attacks would happen. What made the mogul’s innovation so noteworthy was his claim that “The Machine” could predict terrorist attacks before the offenders themselves had even planned them. Reese is the first CIA operative to use this technology to track down individuals, and Person of Interest doesn’t shy away from the moral and ethical implications of this plan.

In fact, throughout its five-season run, Person of Interest never makes it entirely clear whether “The Machine” is a good idea at all, and modern real-life policing has only made the show’s predictions seem tame in comparison. Where The Machine was designed to avoid prejudiced policing, real-life predictive algorithms used by the police rely on racially biased data from existing police reports.

While Person of Interest had a villainous AI that tracked civilians without their consent, real-life private companies have created this infrastructure and currently license these technologies out to law enforcement agencies, from police departments to ICE, to monitor civilians with no criminal record. Where The Machine almost never makes any mistakes, real-life facial recognition software is notorious for often falsely identifying innocent civilians, especially people of color.

Although Prime Video’s superhero satire The Boys became infamous for accidentally predicting real-life events in its comedic storytelling, Person of Interest was alarmingly prescient in the show’s depictions of policing developments that ran roughshod over the rights of civilians. However, where Finch was transparent about how The Machine works, the private companies that run real-life surveillance tech offer no transparency over oversight.

While The Machine was used to save ordinary civilians from terrorism, real-life policing technologies are used for immigration enforcement, avoiding low-level work, and tracking civilians without their consent. Thus, if Person of Interest’s story got anything wrong, it was assuming these technologies would come from caring, troubled geniuses, and not from for-profit private companies who aren’t answerable to anyone.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3385. Anya Taylor-Joy’s 93-Minute Crime Thriller 'Thoroughbreds' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Streaming

One of the most unsung releases of the last decade was 2017’s Thoroughbreds, a thriller deep in the film noir mode with three great actors going toe to toe. With Anya Taylor-Joy, Olivia Cooke, and Anton Yelchin as the architects and participants of a murder plot, it’s less a crime movie and more of a character study, with director Cory Finley mining both pathos and extremely dark comedy from the premise. In an era where minimal-location movies about the sociopathy of the rich were frequently successful discourse machines (including Taylor-Joy’s 2022 vehicle The Menu), Thoroughbreds was a classically amoral story of kids whose wealth insulates them from consequences, yet you still root for them. The movie was unfortunately ahead of the curve with its note-perfect plotting and criminal ideation, as well as its cast.

While the late Anton Yelchin had found major success in movies like Green Room or even the modern Star Trek films, Cooke and Taylor-Joy were just getting started, some years away from the blockbuster extravaganzas of Dune and House of the Dragon. Coming some years before that, Thoroughbreds suggested great depth from all three actors, playing them against each other as they all fight for their own agendas, while also giving viewers the chance to identify with potentially evil teens. The movie is leaving Starz on November 30, but its study of youthful sociopathy and the tenuous nature of female friendship means it should remain a cult classic for years to come.

Thoroughbreds is a movie of interiors, specializing in the rich, old money homes of its protagonists Amanda (Olivia Cooke) and Lily (Anya Taylor-Joy), who live in suburban Connecticut. From the very beginning, when Amanda mercy-kills her crippled horse (leading to the title) in an unnerving moment, the movie keeps its distance from the characters, with director Cory Finley’s camera holding on scenes and moments for long stretches. Rather than the aspirational gleeful immorality of the classic teenage murderer movie Heathers, Thoroughbreds is methodical and ironic. The fancy decor, the emotional repression, and the basement tanning beds all go hand in hand with Amanda’s claims of an inability to feel anything. You might wonder if she’s just being an edgy teenager, especially after the horse euthanizing moment. But the movie’s visual language backs her up.

In a twist directly out of Alfred Hitchcock’s Strangers on a Train, the movie’s narrative begins to hinge on a murderous favor. Lily, effectively tasked by Amanda’s mom to befriend her troubled daughter, has an abusive stepfather named Mark (Paul Sparks), and Amanda, in her emotionless wisdom, presents a solution: kill him. The girls have a means of laundering the murder in the form of drug dealer Tim (Yelchin). Olivia Cooke’s portrayal of Amanda veers beyond creating an empathetic version of somebody suffering from an undisclosed mental illness, but it never goes into villain territory either. The movie’s cold and heavily adorned visual sensibility might have Yorgos Lanthimos-esque ironic distance from what you see, but it means that the relationship between the two girls becomes increasingly complex, in a way that it wouldn’t be if viewers were directly keyed into how the girls see each other.

Cory Finley had reportedly envisioned the movie as a play originally, and that feeling lingers in the film. The minimal cast and locations, as well as the long takes and reliance on dialogue, have the potential to feel theatrical, but the movie is sophisticated on the level of cinematic storytelling, commenting on its cast with its staging and using its widescreen compositions for both comedy and terror as chickens come home to roost. As he told IndieWire, the story began with the idea of a character who couldn’t feel anything. As the friend seeking to take advantage of that to help her own family situation, Anya Taylor-Joy’s Lily is effectively not much different.

The movie’s cinematic lineage is rich, drawing from Alfred Hitchcock (besides Strangers on a Train, his highly theatrical one-take experiment Rope, with its homoerotic murder conspiracy, has a clear line to Thoroughbreds) as well as ‘90s evil rich kid movies like Cruel Intentions, but with a much less moral stance. Peter Jackson’s true-crime classic Heavenly Creatures also feels like an influence, with the fantastical sequences substituted for cold stylization. When Amanda and Lily’s plans go awry, we see the truth of what the girls are willing to go through with, how calculating they can be with the other’s emotional headspace. A different movie about teenage murder conspirators might let them off the hook, but Amanda’s dreams of wild thoroughbred horses suggest that a cruel end is coming to everybody.
