#3383. How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

[Editor’s note: The following story contains minor spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

A few years ago, Quentin Tarantino was set to direct one last movie to fulfill his self-imposed ten film limit before riding off into the sunset. And while he was open about his desire to stay creative in other mediums, not even the most outside-the-box thinkers would have predicted that his next big screen project would be a Netflix movie he wrote for David Fincher. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unlikely miracle that emerged for a few distinct reasons: Tarantino’s hesitance to commit to his final directing effort, Brad Pitt‘s determination to play Cliff Booth again and his longtime friendship with David Fincher, and of course, the collapse of Tarantino’s planned film “The Movie Critic.” Related Stories Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It Danielle Brooks Shares Insights from the Indie Success of ‘If I Go Will They Miss Me’

Given that “The Movie Critic” was also reportedly set in 1970s Los Angeles, and Pitt had signed on to reprise his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” role, there was always going to be speculation about that script turning into “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Tarantino pours gasoline on that flame in the new film when Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the Hollywood manager who serves as both a foil and love interest to Booth, reveals that she used to be a film critic before moving into talent representation. The revelation is not crucial to the plot, though it does provide some clever character development as she explains her view that all movies are the culinary equivalent of hamburgers: enjoyable, but not worthy of serious analysis. Yet the inclusion of those lines kicked off a treasure hunt for fans of a director whose unmade movies are almost as legendary as the ones he actually shot.

A definitive answer to the question of “How much of ‘The Movie Critic’ made it into ‘Cliff Booth?'” is going to be hard to come by. Tarantino scripts are some of the most closely guarded secrets in Hollywood, and even the attached actors are often kept in the dark about scenes that don’t concern them. (In an interview with IndieWire, Debicki denied knowing anything about “The Movie Critic,” and everything we know about Tarantino’s process suggests that she was telling the truth.) Beyond that, reports about “The Movie Critic” suggest that the project was constantly changing, even as it neared the planned start of production. It’s impossible to know about every iteration of the project that may have existed at one point or another, but we can use the history of on-the-record quotes and credible reporting about “The Movie Critic” to make an educated guess about where it ended and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” began.

Cinephiles spent much of 2023 and 2024 receiving piecemeal updates on what was supposed to be Tarantino’s farewell effort. When the project was first reported in March 2023, all we had was the title and a rumor that it was based on legendary New Yorker film critic Pauline Kael. But two months later, Tarantino began to reveal plot details that suggested it was actually inspired by an unnamed film critic who wrote for a magazine he stocked in the porn theaters that he used to work at.

“All the other stuff was too skanky to read, but then there was this porno rag that had a really interesting movie page,” Tarantino said in a May 2025 interview with Deadline. “He wrote about mainstream movies, and he was the second-string critic. I think he was a very good critic. He was as cynical as hell. His reviews were a cross between early Howard Stern and what Travis Bickle might be if he were a film critic. Think about Travis’ diary entries.”

Tarantino went on to say that the movie would take place in Los Angeles in 1977 (just like “Cliff Booth” eventually does) and would take inspiration from the critic’s real life, though the porno rag he wrote for would be fictionalized as The Popstar Pages. The director explained that he had done research on the largely unknown writer’s life, saying that “He wrote like he was 55 but he was only in his early to mid-30s. He died in his late thirties. It wasn’t clear for a while but now I’ve done some more research and I think it was complications due to alcoholism.” He also added that the role would have gone to an American man in his mid-30s, with rumors that Paul Walter Hauser was up for the part.

Tarantino said that the film, which was set up with his “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” backers at Sony, was set to begin “pre-pre-production” in June 2023, and the film secured a California tax credit to shoot the following year. But by April 2024, Tarantino officially scrapped the project. A blockbuster report in THR detailed the many creative changes that “The Movie Critic” went through during its tumultuous year of pre-production. Pitt’s involvement was never in doubt, but the report says that Tarantino looked at multiple ways of incorporating stars of his previous films like John Travolta and Jamie Foxx. He reportedly considered introducing the concept that his movies like “Pulp Fiction” and “Django Unchained” were real ’70s films that existed in this universe, possibly shooting new sequences from movies-within-movies or having his stars show up as the actors who played those characters. There was also an idea that they would interact with a teenage movie theater usher who would be a Sammy Fabelman-style stand-in for a young Tarantino.

None of which happens in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” Debicki’s character says that she wrote movie reviews for a grocery store circular, not a porno rag, and she has far more Pauline Kael than Travis Bickle or Howard Stern in her. And it’s hard to imagine that her and Hauser are ever up for the same parts. The only returning Tarantino characters are Booth and Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate, who appears in a commercial for his signature fake brand Red Apple Cigarettes. But it’s not hard to see how this film could have emerged from the ashes of that one.

When you put all of the reporting about “The Movie Critic” together, it appears that the only constants were Tarantino’s desire to revisit the vintage L.A. world of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” bring back Cliff Booth, and illustrate how working in a movie theater and watching ’70s cinema shaped his worldview and his future. The project collapsed because he couldn’t settle on a story that would incorporate all of those elements while containing enough gravity to serve as his directorial mic drop. But regardless of how many specific plot details from “The Movie Critic” survived the transition to “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” all of those elements are present in the movie opening this week.

The film opens with a movie-within-a-movie, a fictional blaxploitation effort starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II. From there, we see that Cliff is working as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema, where he also conducts some of his shadier business after hours. He does tell two of his teenage concession stand workers that their young age means it’s time to clock out — if you squint hard enough, that might be considered an Easter Egg about Tarantino’s youth and his possible inclusion in “The Movie Critic,” but the brief encounter hardly makes them seem like stand-ins for a man who loves to memorialize himself.

In a recent interview with Empire, Fincher said that he and Pitt each played a role in cutting 60 pages from the 230-page script that Tarantino initially turned in, resulting in a movie that took place in his sprawling world but was shaped by the type of movie that his two collaborators wanted to make. Looking through that lens, a plausible story for how one movie turned into another begins to take shape.

If you believe all of the reporting, it seems clear enough that Tarantino scrapped “The Movie Critic” because he had more vibes than plot. And “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” provides those exact vibes in droves. We’ll never be able to truly know how many elements were carried over unless Tarantino ever releases or novelizes his “Movie Critic” script (and even then, we won’t be able to fully trust that he didn’t make changes over the subsequent years.) But the safest guess is that he took the idea of Brad Pitt wandering through a darker, sleazier version of L.A. than the hippie paradise he inhabited a decade earlier and simply replaced the plans to make a grand statement about cinema with a pulpy crime plot that could have been ripped from one of his beloved Elmore Leonard novels. And the film still devotes plenty of time to showing scenes from fictional ’70s movies and TV shows, so Tarantino still had a chance to indulge that impulse.

The only other factor that can’t be dismissed is the possibility of self-referential trolling. Tarantino might love talking about movies more than he loves watching them. His insistence on retiring after ten films has nothing to do with his own enjoyment of the filmmaking process — in his own words, he simply doesn’t want anyone studying his future filmography to declare that he got washed up at the end of his career. Anyone who factors the opinions of future podcasters into his own major life decisions is deeply aware of what people say about him, and it’s possible that he simply included the lines about Karen’s career as a critic to add to the mythology about one of his legendary unmade movies. For all we know, the fact that IndieWire published this essay and you read it could be the exact reaction he wanted. In that case, well played, Mr. Tarantino.

“The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is now playing in IMAX theaters. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

#3382. The Wallet-Sized Xteink X4 Pro Is Lifehacker's E-Reader Gift of the Year, and It's on Sale for Black Friday

I've read more than 30 books in the past year, all of them on an e-reader with a screen roughly the size of a credit card. If you think that sounds untenable, I say: Don't knock it 'til you've tried it. Once you're immersed in a book, you'll find the size doesn't matter, and the convenience of being able to slip it into any pocket and forget it's there means you need never be without it.

Right now, the Xteink X4 Pro, the best tiny e-reader I've tried so far—and Lifehacker's pick for the 2026 E-Reader Gift of the Year—is on its best sale yet for Black Friday: When ordered directly from Xteink, you'll save 15% off the usual $99 price, bringing it down to $84. This is the cheapest e-reader with a light and a touchscreen that you can buy right now, and it's well worth the money.

The X4 Pro is the newest and best e-reader from Xteink, the Chinese tech startup that turned the e-reading world upside down last year with the launch of the original X4 pocket e-reader. While the X4 Pro is the same size as the basic X4 Classic, it adds two big upgrades—a temperature-adjustable front light and a touchscreen—plus a faster processor and more memory. As a result, it costs a bit more, but you can pick one at a $15 discount right now. (Even at full retail, the X4 Pro is $50 cheaper than the entry-level Kindle after its recent price increase—and even considering the Kindle's current Black Friday discount).

Meanwhile, if you're a reader who prioritizes the crispest text over conveniences like a front light, the 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic and the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 are about $30 less during Amazon's own Black Friday sale.

As much as I love them, these minuscule e-readers aren't for everyone. Some may indeed find the screen too small (though if you've ever read a book on a phone, the experience is similar). Then there's the fact that they can't load your existing libraries of Kindle books; you'll need to source copies of e-books lacking Digital Rights Management (DRM) software. But if you can jump those hurdles, you might just discover it's the weirdest, most lovable piece of tech you've used in years.

#3381. Will Siri AI threaten Apple’s environmental target, given Google and Meta admissions?

I think Apple can reasonably claim to be the leading tech giant when it comes to its environmental credentials. It has led the way with its use of renewable energy, made significant strides with carbon-neutral production, and removed plastic from all its packaging.

All of this could potentially be put at risk by the company’s ambitions for Siri AI, however, as Meta joins Google in admitting it is now unlikely to meet its own 2030 net zero promise, thanks to the huge power demands of the data centers powering its AI services …

Apple’s environmental record isn’t entirely perfect. For example, when it claimed that the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 were carbon neutral back in 2023, that claim was described as “bogus,” with the EU banning Apple from repeating it. The company has also been criticized for pushing a relentless annual iPhone cycle, encouraging frequent upgrades.

Overall, however, Apple has first-rate credentials when it comes to the environment. It was way back in 2018 when the company hit its goal of running its own operations off 100% renewable energy. This includes all Apple facilities, from Apple Park through data centers to its worldwide retail store network.

I said at the time that using more environmentally friendly packaging should be the company’s next priority, and it has indeed made great progress with this over the years, succeeding in removing all plastic packaging earlier this year.

After its own operations, Apple set about trying to tackle the power usage of its manufacturing partners. Back in 2020, the company set a goal of having its entire supply chain be carbon neutral by 2030. Just four years later, Apple said it was 95% of the way there.

The company also helps fund and support a wide range of environmental initiatives around the world. Just a few examples include conservation in China’s national parks, environmental protection and carbon removal in Australia and New Zealand, and helping to fund the build-out of renewable energy capacity in India.

Potentially, however, the vast energy demands of the data centers powering AI services could put its 2030 goal at risk. Other tech giants have already admitted that it may lead them to fail to hit their own renewable energy promises.

Back in 2024, for example, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said that the AI boom was “challenging” to the company’s 2030 carbon-free goal. CNET reports that Meta is now also admitting that it may fail to hit the same target.

Meta’s data center and sustainability chiefs wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets.” In an emailed statement to CNET, a Meta spokesperson added, “We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline.”

Notably, a lot of Siri’s most advanced AI capabilities are currently powered by Google’s Gemini models.

At the same 2024 event where Google expressed doubts, Apple reiterated its commitment to its 2030 target. Then-CEO Tim Cook repeated this assurance later the same year, although admitted it would be challenging.

More challenges, yes. But are we coming off the goal? No, definitely not. With more data centers, you use more renewable energy, and we’ve built that muscle now […] I feel very good about 2030.

In the company’s most recent environmental progress report, it said that it was was still using 100% renewable energy despite using over 2.5 billion kWh of electricity to power its data centers.

We’re proud that 100 percent of that electricity came from renewable sources including solar, wind, and low-impact hydropower. To cover our needs, we build our own renewable power projects and work with utilities to purchase clean energy from locally obtained resources. We’re staying at 100 percent even as Apple’s data center capacity continues to grow.

The same report said the company had achieved zero water use for cooling at its latest data centers.

At our three newest data centers, we use high-efficiency air-cooled chillers instead of water-cooled systems, resulting in zero water use for cooling.

However, the greatest challenge for Apple lies ahead. The reason that Google and Meta are now backtracking on their promises is that both companies now have massive AI capabilities. As yet, Apple does not.

What happens as Apple expands Siri AI capabilities as usage increases, and as the company moves into agentic AI features? Is it realistic for the company to maintain its 100% track record with vastly greater data center energy usage?

Greenpeace expressed its own doubts earlier this year.

“AI will be the defining test of Apple’s climate commitments,” spokesperson Avex Li says. “To preserve Tim Cook’s environmental legacy, the company will need to show that AI growth can be accommodated within its existing climate commitments through absolute emissions reductions, additional renewable energy investment, and longer-lasting products.”

Apple did not respond directly but merely pointed to its past statements and most recent environmental progress report.

I don’t doubt the company’s desire to maintain its track record, but if Apple does join the likes of Google and Meta in becoming a major AI player, sticking to its 2030 timing is going to become increasingly difficult.

Do you think Apple will succeed? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3379. 'The Last of Us' Meets 'Silo' in Hulu’s 4-Part Sci-Fi Thriller

Post-apocalyptic sci-fi thrillers have become some of TV's best shows. With examples like The Last of Us or Silo, these stories have grown incredibly popular for their spectacle and epic tales. The genre is more than gruesome stories about the world ending, as it offers a deep exploration of universal human struggles. While these recent examples have earned considerable attention, and rightfully so, they are not the first. In fact, Snowpiercer took a similar approach in 2020. The series creates an immersive world full of danger and division that all fans of the genre should watch.

Snowpiercer delivers a unique premise and incredible worldbuilding that sets it apart. Inspired by the 2013 film of the same name, the story isn't totally original, but the series builds on the concept that always deserved more than two hours. And Snowpiercer certainly expands the idea with four unforgettable seasons. Though it may not have gained the popularity that other comparable series have, it still deserves attention. Six years later, Snowpiercer is the perfect binge watch for anyone who loves sci-fi thrillers, dystopian worlds, or complex moral questions.

Snowpiercer features a world like no other, where a massive luxury train is the only place people can live. Eerily set in 2026, the story takes place seven years after an environmental disaster created a new ice age, killing much of human civilization. However, some survive on a constantly moving train designed by eccentric billionaire Mr. Joseph Wilford (Sean Bean). While the movement keeps them alive, the survivors continue to struggle. The system is strictly divided into distinct social classes. The elite live in the front, third-class laborers keep the machine running, and the stowaways, known as the Tailies, are just trying to survive. However, the dynamic alters when a series of murders threatens the train. Head Engineer Melanie Cavill (Jennifer Connelly) pulls Chicago police officer Andre Layton (Daveed Diggs) up from the Tail to uncover the truth.

Layton has his own motivations. He dreams of revolution and believes this investigation can take him one step closer, allowing him to map out the train. However, the fallout spirals as the train is full of secrets. Most prominently, the passengers begin to realize that inventor Joseph Wilford isn't running the train because Melanie abandoned him during boarding, leaving him for dead. Although this society is confined to a train, Snowpiercer covers a lot of ground as it explores the brutal realities of civilization, oppression, and unavoidable moral questions of survival. This is the crux of the series, giving it a dark and fascinating tone.

What stands out most about Snowpiercer is its worldbuilding. A train is an uncharacteristic setting, but it comes with plenty to explore as the series delves into how different biomes separate the classes, how food is grown, and even how the passengers deal with their dead. These may seem like small details, but they reveal a lot about the world and the desperate characters who inhabit it. Through these elements, the series brings this society to life and creates something new. As the story goes on, Snowpiercer even explores beyond the train, showing the devastation of the icy world and further immersing the audience in the dystopian setting.

Idris Elba has fans on the edges of their train seats.

Though this concept is rare, the story is inspired by the movie, but the two are far from the same. Of course, there are similarities, but Snowpiercer isn't even strictly a remake. The series takes the concept, but uses different characters and circumstances to tell its own story. With significantly more time, the series sets a slower pace, building tension and introducing the world a little at a time, which is a luxury the film doesn't have. Ultimately, that dedication to the story is what makes Snowpiercer work. The series stands out, even as the dystopian genre grows, and though it's a few years old now, Snowpiercer is an unmatched sci-fi watch that deserves more attention.

Snowpiercer is streaming on Hulu in the U.S.

AirPods Pro 3 (now only $149, down from $249) offer many advantages over AirPods Pro 2, but after a year of use, the improvements to Active Noise Cancellation alone have proven worth the upgrade.

These new features are nice to have, but Active Noise Cancellation is where AirPods Pro 3 become a major upgrade. Apple says it’s “the world’s best in-ear Active Noise Cancellation.” Here’s how the new ANC compares to previous models:

I spend nearly my entire workday with AirPods Pro 3 in my ears. Whether I’m working from home with young kids around or at a busy coffee shop, I rely on ANC to block out background noise and help me focus.

One reason I’ve been especially impressed with the ANC upgrades is that I didn’t have any real complaints about ANC on AirPods Pro 2. But Apple managed to deliver improvements in AirPods Pro 3 I had no idea I needed, and when I’ve tried going back to AirPods Pro 2 I couldn’t believe how much noise was let in.

If Active Noise Cancellation is important to you, I highly recommend AirPods Pro 3.

#3377. ‘The Hunting Wives’ Review: Season 2 Reloads Without Slowing Down in Netflix’s Delirious Soap

Amid all the sex and murder in “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 — and there is a lot of sex and murder — the riskiest scene suspends itself between the two. Sophie (Brittany Snow), an East Coast liberal out of place in the conservative Texas town of Maple Brook, and Margo (Malin Åkerman), the mysterious local matriarch who can wrap just about anyone around her finely manicured fingertips, are confronted with a fresh dilemma. For spoilers sake, I won’t get into specifics, but the issue is urgent and impacts them both, without being serious enough to warrant what turns out to be their first-thought fix:

In the moment, their lethal instinct seems reasonable. Margo already shot a pregnant teenager in the woods, and Sophie committed vehicular homicide against Margo’s brother (which invited suspicions about Sophie’s past, considering its eerie similarities to a deadly “accident” back in Massachusetts). Their friends, neighbors, and even a youth pastor met their maker, too — just in the first season! So what’s one more body to bury? Go on! Kill ’em! Get yours! Related Stories ‘The Lowdown’ Season 2 Finale Hinges on Two Monologues — Let Ethan Hawke and Sterlin Harjo Break Them Down Will Ferrell Golf Comedy ‘The Hawk’ Canceled at Netflix After Just One Season

But before their bloodlust gets the best of them, their better angels make one last plea. Margo hesitates. Sophie follows suit. The gears start turning as they stare into each other’s wide, worried eyes: Are they really prepared to take another life? Are people that disposable to them? What does their initial response say about how they’ve changed? What does it mean about who they’ve become?

No need to spoil what happens next. The pause makes all the difference. “The Hunting Wives” has always been self-aware, but Margo and Sophie’s recognition of slaughter as their default response to trouble is a critical moment in a second season that reloads without slowing down. Creator Rebecca Cutler knows her Netflix soap is careening past the point where its central couple can reasonably return to lives lived between Margarita Mondays and Sunday church. Killing again, so quickly and carelessly, puts them on the precipice of becoming Bonnie and Clyde Bonnie — known fugitives who are only out for each other. Taking a beat lends the series a critical perspective — a vantage point from the top of the roller coaster, right before the big drop, where you can appreciate for a few brief, fleeting seconds the insanity to come.

Then you’re flying. You (and Margo and Sophie) are convinced it’s better to just move forward. Heck, this crisis isn’t going to fix itself!

Margo and Sophie’s breakneck pace to break necks is mostly a feature in Netflix’s surprise hit. The high-key camp comedy and low-key conservative satire moves quickly, sure, but where its characters are often flustered and panicked, it’s decisive in a way that exudes confidence. Progress is fast but assured. The drama is elevated but mindful. Characters don’t ask for permission or forgiveness; they just go after what they want, what they need, or what they feel they have to have, creating a propulsive viewing experience that zips by in a (muzzle) flash.

It’s a welcome change from prestige dramas that regularly feel like they’re stalling for time. While other shows tout firearms around for so long it’s like they’ve never heard of Chekhov, the hunting wives pull the trigger like they’re expecting money to come out — or lovers. Before you can think, “Wait, are they gay, too?” the person in question is already bending their same-sex partner over a desk. Even Season 2’s in-media-res opening lasts only a few seconds — like it’s flipping the bird to streaming TV’s favorite plot device — giving just the briefest glimpse of cop cars racing up to a giant cabin where Margo is (supposedly) being held hostage and Sophie is (supposedly) with her, holding a gun.

The opening tease only gets funnier as you find out how much unfolds between the start of the season and the flash-forward, especially considering its implication — that Sophie would threaten Margo’s life — makes sense from the start. Sophie begins Season 2 trying to repair her marriage to Graham (Evan Jonigkeit) and distance herself from Margo. The former goal sees her going to counseling sessions (where she comically compares her family to a box she wants to be trapped in), running errands, and playing the dutiful housewife.

The latter goal is harder and, arguably, more important. Margo doesn’t know her brother is dead. He’s not answering her calls or texts, but that’s hardly unprecedented behavior, so Margo ignores it — until the leader of a motorcycle gang (Dale Dickey!) shows up, claiming Kyle owes her, and if he doesn’t pay, she’ll take what she wants from Margo.

There’s never a good time for angry bikers to roar up your driveway demanding money, but it’s a particularly bad time for Margo. She’s in the doghouse with Jed (Dermot Mulroney) over the whole “a high schooler got me pregnant and then I had an abortion” issue, but a) that means she’s living in the pool house, not the poor house, and b) he’s really only mad because it’s a potential threat to his run for governor, which is gaining steam. Margo tries calling and texting Sophie, but she’s not answering. She wants to believe she doesn’t need Margo, love Margo, that she maybe even hates Margo. But a few cleverly laced connections make it clear she can’t.

Outside our core couple, Season 2 introduces plenty of plotlines that could pull them together and/or tear them apart. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman) doesn’t see why welcoming a camera crew to film her friends for a reality show (“Married Justice”) could lead to problems, even when the flirty producer warns participants that they should assume they’re “always on camera.” Her husband and co-star, Sheriff Jonny (Branton Box), is just as foolishly carefree, despite Deputy Wanda (Karen Rodriguez) investigating another dead girl in the woods — aka giving Callie a reason to ask questions about the last dead girl in Maple Brook, aka the aforementioned pregnant high schooler Margo killed.

Speaking of people Margo would prefer to forget, her former boy-toy Brad (George Ferrier), is having a hard time at Baylor. He can’t get over the recent murder of his mother, and his lonely boy coping mechanisms (playing acoustic guitar) soon attract the wrong kind of attention: a predatory music mogul named Chase (John Stamos) who promises to make Brad forget all his worries by turning him into a star (right after he loads him up with booze and drugs).

How Cutler shifts the puzzle pieces around to exert pressure proves just as engaging as before. There are plenty of big, loud laughs to go along with a steady supply of sly jokes and juicy melodrama. Anyone tuning in for the soap should be satisfied, just as anyone eager for some edgy satire should find it.

So long as they’re as open as these characters. “The Hunting Wives” may don MAGA drag to tell its story, but it’s a savage critique of conservative values. There’s Brad’s holier-than-thou father, Reverend Clint (Jason Davis), whose over-reliance on Old Testament discipline masks a hands-off parenting style that feeds his desperate son to the wolves. There’s Jed’s hypocritical right-wing politician, who’s more than OK with a little murder if it helps his campaign (knowing his constituents wouldn’t hold it against him) but can’t abide by his wife’s emotional outbursts in the pursuit of personal independence.

Then there’s the fun fact that everyone is gay (or bi or curious). So much of the show’s tension stems from secret trysts that only need to stay secret because of Maple Brook’s pervasive intolerance. That goes double for Sophie and Margo, whose continued pursuit of their repressed desires manifests in bigger and bigger risks. They get a small taste of what their lives could be like if they could just follow their hearts, sans consequence, forever, and then someone comes along to remind them why they can’t. It so often feels like there’s no real hope for the life they want that they fight like hell for whatever sliver they think they can sustain.

That fight gives the series its heart and its haste, but not everything fares better at a high velocity. By season’s end, Margo and Sophie’s individual interiority is rooted in too many questions and not enough answers, while their relationship feels more symbolic than genuine. Perhaps that’s the point. Perhaps the couple isn’t fated to be together as much as they’re fated to go further alone. Perhaps their relationship is more of a means to an end; a reminder of how far off track they got when they were isolated, and how hard it is to get back on track when the world is working to keep them apart.

Either way, it’s good drama. Either way, they’re going to discover new sides of themselves. Either way, the coaster is already racing ahead. Maybe it jumps the tracks, maybe it doesn’t. Maybe after all that, they really should just keep killing.

“The Hunting Wives” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 26 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3375. iOS 27 basically turns your iPhone and AirPods into an Apple Watch at the gym

GymKit has been one of Apple Watch’s smartest fitness features since it launched in 2017. Tap your watch to compatible gym equipment, and Apple Watch shares your heart rate while the machine sends back metrics like distance, incline, pace, and calories.

With iOS 27, Apple is expanding that idea beyond Apple Watch. I tested the new GymKit on iPhone and AirPods Pro 3 ($149, reg. $249) experience with a GymKit-compatible treadmill. It basically gives you the Apple Watch GymKit workout tracking experience, just without the watch. This could be useful in a lot of scenarios.

The setup is simple. I tapped my iPhone to the treadmill, picked Indoor Walk (Indoor Run is also offered), and started the workout from the treadmill. With GymKit, workout data is stored privately on iPhone and removed from the equipment.

Once the workout started, the treadmill received heart-rate data from AirPods Pro 3. Meanwhile, the Fitness app on iPhone received the treadmill’s distance, pace, incline, and calorie data. Treadmills know details that an iPhone and AirPods can’t know on their own, especially incline and precise belt distance.

As a side note: Apple Watch has more accurate treadmill workout tracking as part of watchOS 27. GymKit remains the gold standard for accurate data, though.

GymKit also avoids two awkward gym habits. You don’t need to hold the treadmill’s metal heart-rate contacts while jogging. You also do not need to wear a Bluetooth heart-rate strap.

AirPods Pro 3 become the heart-rate source (and likely your podcast or music audio source as well). iPhone becomes the workout computer, which you can monitor during your workout. And the treadmill fills in the machine data while providing the surface for walking or running.

Apple has been moving more fitness features onto iPhone for years. iOS first made the Fitness app useful without Apple Watch as Apple Fitness+ leaned into iPhone as an entry point. AirPods Pro 3 pushed that further as the first AirPods with heart-rate tracking, after Apple tested the idea with Powerbeats Pro 2.

iOS 27 brings those pieces together. GymKit on iPhone shouldn’t replace Apple Watch for people who wear one every day. Instead, it’s a great backup when your Apple Watch is dead, charging, or left at home.

It also gives iPhone and AirPods users a taste of the Apple Watch experience, which could attract future Apple Watch customers.

In testing with iOS 27 beta 1, my Exercise ring didn’t update as I worked out without wearing Apple Watch. But after I put my watch back on, the Exercise ring caught up, and the workout appeared in Fitness with the right data.

My sample 16-minute treadmill walk showed 0.66 miles, 65 active calories, 97 total calories, 32 feet of elevation gain, and a 115 BPM average heart rate, just like if I’d worn an Apple Watch.

I had been getting the impression that gym equipment manufacturers had been abandoning GymKit support - if they ever had done so initially. I even got the impression that the majority of equipment in Apple's own onsite Gym at the Apple Park may not have supported it - at least originally.

Does Apple have a webpage listing compatible brands and models? Like they do/did for HomeKit.

What is other people perception? Any rowing machines that support it?

…checks - surprisingly it looks like Peloton do support it on their bikes.

If I tried to use GymKit on iPhone without AirPods, the iPhone disconnected when the workout started because it had no heart-rate source. If I tried to start GymKit from iPhone while wearing Apple Watch, iOS pointed me back to the Workout app on Apple Watch instead, though you can continue without using the watch.

GymKit on iPhone is one of those iOS 27 features that sounds small until it solves a real problem. If Apple Watch is your default workout tracker, it probably stays that way.

But if your watch dies or you forget it at home, iPhone plus AirPods Pro 3 can now log a treadmill workout with real heart-rate data and real treadmill metrics.

#3373. 8 Elite HBO Miniseries to Binge Right Now

HBO has long had a reputation for prestige, cinematic shows and miniseries. But the network has come a long way since The Far Pavilions and has become synonymous with top-tier, critically acclaimed miniseries. Several of the miniseries that HBO has produced over the last couple of decades are not just another feather in their hat but icons of their genre, TV classics of their time, and standouts among their contemporaries.

While 2001’s Band of Brothers has become the gold standard for war-drama television, 2019’s Chernobyl excels in translating a traumatic human event into an intricate character study. Between adaptations of bestselling novels and intriguing original stories, here are our picks for elite HBO miniseries that you can binge right now.

Scottish comedian and actor Richard Gadd of Baby Reindeer fame returns with another chilling miniseries, Half Man, which he also writes and stars in. The six-part psychological thriller unspools the complicated, violent, lifelong friendship between Gadd’s Ruben and Jamie Bell’s Niall, after an unexpected incident at Niall’s wedding forces them to reconnect with their past. Stuart Campbell and Mitchell Robertson portray the younger versions of Ruben and Niall.

Half Man is a story about toxic male friendships, but it is the show’s treatment that makes it more intense and raw than most. While Niall is an intricately written character, Ruben is a drastic departure from Gadd’s fragile, sensitive role in Baby Reindeer, and the actor-comedian thrives as the aggressive, tormented character. Deeply disturbing yet delicate in its own way, Half Man is an exceptionally intense show that easily ranks among the best TV dramas made in the 2020s.

Created by Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks in their second collaboration following Saving Private Ryan, Band of Brothers is a 21st-century television classic adapted from the non-fiction book by Stephen E. Ambrose. Set during WWII, the war drama recounts the story of the “Easy” Company, 2nd Battalion, 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the 101st Airborne Division of the US Army on the Western Front between D-Day and their occupation of Berchtesgaden. Kirk Acevedo, Eion Bailey, Damian Lewis, Ron Livingston, and Neal McDonough portray various real-life characters.

Band of Brothers became an instant classic when it premiered 25 years ago and has since been an HBO landmark and often cited as a benchmark of the genre. The 10-episode miniseries combines a dramatized narrative with documentary-style, candid interviews with real veterans, reconstructing one of the grimmest times of human history in the most thoughtful way. A remarkable tribute to the sacrifices of a whole generation of American soldiers, Band of Brothers is surely a must-watch for genre fans.

Created by David Simon, Ed Burns, and Evan Wright, Generation Kill is an often-forgotten war miniseries that adapts Wright’s non-fiction book of the same name, chronicling his experiences as an embedded reporter in the US Marine Corps during the 2003 Invasion of Iraq. Set during the first phase of the war, the series follows Wright, played by Lee Tergesen, as he rides along with the U.S. Marine Corps' 1st Reconnaissance Battalion on their way to Baghdad. Other real-life people are portrayed by Alexander Skarsgård, Billy Rush, James Ransone, and Stark Sands.

Generation Kill is often considered one of the most visceral and grounded portrayals of war on television. At the time of its broadcast, it was among the most prestigious shows of the genre and is undeniably one of the best war shows of the 2000s. However, despite its critical acclaim and several accolades, Generation Kill has mostly faded from mainstream attention and has been overshadowed by bigger productions.

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

Created by David E. Kelley, The Undoing is loosely based on Jean Hanff Korelitz’s novel You Should Have Known and follows Grace (Nicole Kidman), a wealthy therapist in New York City, whose perfect life begins to unravel when her renowned oncologist husband, Dr. Jonathan Fraser (Hugh Grant), is accused of murder. As the investigation proceeds, Grace and her family learn shocking truths about Jonathan, making her question her marriage, profession, and the truth of her life. Other key cast members include Noma Dumezweni, Édgar Ramírez, Donald Sutherland, and Noah Jupe.

Elevated by the star power of its cast and refined production design, The Undoing is truly an elite miniseries and one of the finest HBO has produced in the 2020s. Nicole Kidman and Hugh Grant steal every scene with their commanding presence, even if the plot loses momentum occasionally, making this six-episode psychological crime thriller a highly engaging watch. The show has earned praise for its acting, cinematography, and strong plot twists, but has also been criticized for its writing and pacing.

Now considered one of the most immersive screen portrayals of the disaster of 1986, Chernobyl is a dramatized retelling of the titular nuclear plant explosion in Ukraine that resulted in the devastation of all life in the region for decades. The series takes a closer look at the accident from the perspectives of all the key people involved, exploring the events leading up to it and its aftermath. The show boasts a strong ensemble cast, with Jared Harris, Stellan Skarsgård, Emily Watson, Paul Ritter, Jessie Buckley, and more in notable roles.

Created by Craig Mazin, Chernobyl is a masterfully made miniseries that cleverly unpacks the horrific history within its limited runtime. While the show takes some dramatic liberties, trading fact for fiction, it does so engagingly, with powerful performances and an atmospheric setting. The series has since remained a critical darling and a fan favorite, distinctly capturing the emotional and physical intensity of the real tragedy.

Starring Kate Winslet as protagonist Marianne “Mare” Sheehan, Mare of Easttown follows the titular police detective in a small Philadelphia town, where she attempts to solve the murder of a local teenager while being tormented by a similar case from a year ago. Mare continues to search for truth while grappling with past guilt, the loss of a child, divorce, and her declining reputation. Julianne Nicholson, Jean Smart, Angourie Rice, and Guy Pearce also star in key roles.

When Mare of Easttown first premiered, it was a class of its own as a crime drama thriller miniseries. Its gritty story, grounded characters, and deeply emotional plotlines all come together to make this an intense show that is sure to leave an impact on the audience long after the credits roll. Created by Brad Ingelsby, Mare of Easttown has become a modern classic for HBO that thrives on Kate Winslet’s exceptional, award-winning performance, which is often considered her TV best.

Based on Criminal Justice by Peter Moffat and created by Richard Price and Steven Zaillian, The Night Of centers on a Pakistani-American college student named Nasir “Naz” Khan (Riz Ahmed), who wakes up after a nightlong party fueled by drugs and alcohol next to the dead body of a woman he met the night before. With missing memories of the night and evidence pointing to him as the killer, Naz leaves his fate in the hands of a resolute lawyer named John Stone (John Turturro). Bill Camp, Michael Kenneth Williams, and Poorna Jagannathan appear in key roles.

The Night Of is an excellently made crime drama that grips the audience with its tightly-knit plot and deep, character-driven storytelling. The show’s creators elevate the original material by putting an intelligent spin on classic tropes and making it a timely story. When it premiered, the crime thriller was critically praised for its masterful production, layered characterizations, and riveting performances by Turturro and Ahmed.

A Southern Gothic psychological thriller miniseries created by Marti Noxon, Sharp Objects is a series adaptation of Gillian Flynn’s debut novel of the same name and follows Camille Preaker (Amy Adams), a reporter suffering from alcoholism and psychological troubles, who returns to her hometown in Missouri. Recently discharged from a psychiatric hospital and returning to her controlling mother, Adora (Patricia Clarkson), Camille is forced to confront her personal demons while investigating the murder of two young girls. Chris Messina and Eliza Scanlen also have main roles.

The HBO adaptation of Sharp Objects stays true to Flynn’s original crime novel in tone and themes but varies in format and pacing. In fact, the slow-burn storytelling balances the show’s atmospheric setting and dark themes to better explore the characters’ fractured psyches and meditate on their emotional states. Headlined by intense performances from Adams and Clarkson, Sharp Objects is one of HBO's best crime thriller miniseries of the 2010s.

#3370. How Disney’s ‘Hexed’ Reinvents the Witch Through Animation

Every visual element in animation helps tell the story. That’s especially useful when you’re trying to do something new inside the long, proud tradition of Disney animated movies where magic is afoot. “Hexed” is exactly that: the story of a young girl named Billie (Hailee Steinfeld) who learns there’s more to life than her small-town Ohio hometown and more to her family, particularly her mother Alice (Rashida Jones), than meets the eye.

And by “more,” we mean witches. Lots of witches.

“Hexed” builds on work that writers Jared Bush and Dana Ledoux Miller have done with Disney movies like “Encanto” and “Moana,” and that directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Josie Trinidad (along with co-director Jason Hand) have done with “Raya and the Last Dragon” and “Frozen 2,” among others. In a way, much of it feels familiar to recent Disney Animation Studios fare: A secret world of wonder and magic awaits just around the riverbend and/or through a magic portal, accessible only by imbuing one’s inner spark with “witchification.” But there is still something fundamentally broken about that magic world that our protagonist is positioned to make happen. Related Stories How Much of Quentin Tarantino’s Scrapped Film ‘The Movie Critic’ Made It Into ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’? Robert Aramayo’s Star-Making Turn in ‘I Swear’ Is Already Award-Winning, Now He Just Wants People to See It

And by “something,” “Hexed” Celeste (Jodie Foster), the queen of the hidden realm of Hexe, who is waiting to complete a moonlit ritual that will change the world forever.

According to Miller, the “Hexed” team differentiates this world from the magic of others in the Disney Vault through character design. “ If you look at Billie, you look at Alice, and you look at Celeste, I think we see their personalities come forward,” Miller told IndieWire. “With Alice in particular, she wears this impractical, tight, fitted skirt suit. For me, that was always indicative of the way she is trying to control everything around her, including herself. Even the way she does her hair, she is trying to make sure that her world is safe and contained.”

But the world isn’t safe or containable, and that’s part of the character design, too. Billie doesn’t just have a sparkle in her eyes — he has a crescent moon, hinting at the importance she may hold in completing Hexe’s magic.

“The crescent moon was something that was done in Vis Dev, and then the lighting department told us, ‘We can track that all the way through,” Veerasunthorn told IndieWire. “[It hints at] something special and witchy about Billie, even though she doesn’t know that about herself yet. The way that you see her hair curled in the same shape of the crescent moon, too, is speaking to someone who is looking to fulfill her potential.”

Billie’s design, from the reflection of the moon in her eyes to the color and shape of her hair to the natural elements woven into her clothes, hints at her tendency toward witchiness — and toward belonging in a world she doesn’t even know she belongs in. “We as the audience, we can be like, ‘Girl, figure yourself out!’” Veerasunthorn joked.

Both Billie and Alice are designed in stark contrast to Celeste, who perhaps has too much figured out in terms of witch magic and her silvery, flowing, regal appearance. “[Celeste’s] magic is elegant and powerful, very controlled,” Veerasunthorn said. “The color of Alice’s magic is in between these two extremes, and we wanted to get the sense that there’s something broken about her magic that we don’t quite understand yet. There’s a lost-and-found quality, and hopefully subconsciously we’re hoping that she can put her magic back together.”

“What was a challenge was that it’s this world of magic, a world of witches, and we’ve seen that a lot in media,” Trinidad told IndieWire. “We were trying to find our unique take on that world and how we could be modern and fresh and also sort of pay homage to our own Disney legacy.”

One key way “Hexed” speaks to that Disney tradition is by having a powerful queen who blurs the line between what’s best for her and what’s best for the world. Celeste is also [SPOILER] Alice’s mother and Billie grandmother; there’s a long and proud Disney tradition of very complicated abuelas to outright villain grandmothers, which Bush himself has contributed to in the past.

“The worst part is that my own mother, who’s absolutely lovely, is a grandmother now to my three boys, and she is deeply offended by my choices,” Bush joked to IndieWire about what he has against grandmothers, anyway. “I think the only grandma I’ve written that’s been undeniably loving nonstop is Grandma Tala [from ‘Moana’] — and she didn’t survive the movie.”

But Celeste is a collection of influences from the writers’ lives, the Disney storytelling tradition, and wider pop culture — and not least the actor who ended up voicing her. “We were trying to figure [Celeste] out, and the second that Jodie said yes to the role, it changed the entire character. Because, to be honest, when you’re writing for Jodie Foster, that’s nerve-wracking,” Bush said. “We better get this right. We better make this character interesting and layered.”

Bush and Miller’s writing intended to create space between Celeste’s polished appearance and the roiling jealousy and insecurity she’s buried underneath. “She’s a real villain in a way that’s icky and, for me, that’s a really fun thing to write. On top of the fact that she’s this person trying to take power and maintain power any way that she can, she’s also weirdly vulnerable and needy at the same time. It’s this really uncomfortable combination of characteristics that was really fun to write and to see what Jodie would do with it.”

Leaving space in the writing for animation and performance, the collaboration between story and animation teams is a core part of the writing for “Hexed” and all other Disney Animation Studios films. “We sit down with our story artists and with our animators, and we say, for instance, ‘the premise is we’re going to a weird place with a bunch of reject familiars. What could happen there?’ And everyone spitballs, and great ideas rise to the surface,” Bush said. “More than anything, what I love doing is trying to find a fun sandbox and then being really willing to go wherever the great ideas go.”

Bush, Miller, Veerasunthorn, Trinidad, and Hand all told IndieWire that this openness to great ideas is what makes Disney animation so special, and can make even familiar storytelling territory feel fresh and exciting.

“Maybe we’re coming for granddads next,” Bush said.

#3369. New Lee-Child-Recommended Thriller Series Releases January That Reacher Fans Can’t Miss

When it comes to modern thriller book series, Lee Child is an author readers trust more than many others. His rapid-fire rhythmic storytelling, explosive narrative arcs, and heroes with an unwavering sense of justice have captivated fans for decades. His multi-award-winning Jack Reacher novels have come to define the genre in the present day, with Child’s tale of a wandering former military policeman being a literary thriller staple since Reacher made his debut in 1997’s The Killing Floor.

The only problem with the Reacher books is deciding what to read afterward. They’re almost too good. Plenty of thrillers offer violence and conspiracies, but fewer deliver that same combination of gripping action and a protagonist who makes losing oneself in thousands of pages across an entire series feel like light work. Fortunately, Mark Greaney’s The Gray Man novels offer both, and they have an endorsement from Lee Child himself to prove it. For Reacher fans who’ve devoured everything from The Killing Floor to 2026’s Chain Reaction, Greaney’s The Gray Man saga is the perfect next step, especially with a January release giving readers another reason to discover the series’ lethal yet surprisingly principled leading man.

Rather than a military cop turned drifter, The Gray Man books follow Court Gentry, a former CIA operative turned assassin whose extraordinary abilities repeatedly collide with his stubborn moral code. There are 15 published novels so far, starting with 2009’s The Gray Man, providing plenty of dangerous assignments and double-crosses that are bound to delight any Reacher fan. The latest, The Hard Line, reaches US paperback on January 12, 2027. That makes the newest installment in this Barry Award-winning series easier than ever to dive into for Reacher readers seeking a new literary character to obsess over.

Mark Greaney’s The Gray Man novels have attracted plenty of impressive endorsements, but one particularly persuasive recommendation keeps appearing in press releases, blurbs, and book covers: Lee Child’s declaration, “I love the Gray Man.” It’s a short statement with considerable weight. Few authors understand the appeal of a resourceful, dangerous thriller novel protagonist better than Lee Child, and his approval immediately gives Reacher readers a reason to dive into Greaney’s world.

For any fans of Jack Reacher, the explosive sequence of events that unfold once Court Gentry’s enemies start underestimating him are bound to resonate. Both series understand the satisfaction of watching an exceptionally capable outsider dismantle an opponent’s carefully constructed plan. Money, manpower, and official authority offer little protection against characters like Reacher and Gentry, both of whom can identify a weakness and exploit it before anyone realizes what’s happening. Crucially, the intelligence of both heroes matters as much as their capacity for violence. Just like the best Reacher novels, the thrill and joy of The Gray Man books is in seeing how Gentry assesses a seemingly impossible situation, then discovering just how badly their adversaries have misjudged them.

There’s also a moral stubbornness beneath the brutality that makes The Gray Man’s Gentry a character fans of Lee Child’s Jack Reacher are all-but-guaranteed to fall in love with. Gentry’s profession makes him complicated, but his personal code gives readers something solid to hold onto amid shifting loyalties. Like Reacher, he’s endearing because doing the right thing can make his life considerably harder, but that never leads him to compromise his moral values. That tension keeps the momentum high and the action emotionally grounded. Gentry is, just like Reacher, a character readers want him to survive, and it’s because his commitment to doing the right thing makes him someone worth supporting.

However, nobody should be mistaken into thinking that The Gray Man has nothing to distinguish itself. Mark Greaney gives the familiar appeal of the Jack Reacher novels a distinctive espionage setting that sets his own series and characters apart. Where Reacher frequently uncovers trouble in American communities, Gentry operates amid international intelligence networks, covert missions, and betrayals with consequences across borders. Greaney’s extensive research and training with military and law enforcement personnel help give those encounters a substantial level of detail and authenticity. The result is a book series that offers Reacher fans familiar pleasures while opening up a much larger, more treacherous world.

You can purchase The Gray Man, the first book in the series, here.

The run-up January next year is a great time for Reacher fans to start exploring Court Gentry’s world, especially if paperbacks are their go-to format. The Hard Line, the fifteenth and latest The Gray Man novel, arrived in hardcover and ebook through Berkley on February 17, 2026, alongside its audiobook edition. Its US paperback follows on January 12, 2027, nearly eleven months later. For readers who prefer paperbacks, that wait brings a chance to experience one of the best The Gray Man novels without having to carry around a clunky hardback, but with something more physical than an ebook.

The Hard Line has been celebrated by existing fans of The Gray Man because of how deeply personal the latest conspiracy Gentry gets swept up in becomes. Intelligence personnel are being targeted, while Mark Greaney’s globe-trotting hero faces an assassin whose revenge threatens the people he cares about, including his estranged father. The family dynamic gives the danger an emotional force beyond another hazardous white-knuckle assignment.

Gentry’s extraordinary competence can, of course, keep him alive, but protecting everyone around him is a much less certain proposition. The book has been praised for making an established action hero feel vulnerable again. There aren’t really any bad books in The Gray Man series, but The Hard Line’s combination of superb character development and escalating danger has ensured the series’ most recent installment was instantly celebrated as one of its best.

For Reacher readers who like the sound of a spectacle-heavy thriller that doesn’t skimp on serious consequences for its protagonist, January’s rerelease of The Hard Line is bringing considerably more than another collection of gunfights to paperback for the first time.

You can purchase Mark Greaney's The Hard Line here.

#3367. Anya Taylor-Joy’s 2-Hour Thriller Is Still Her Greatest Movie 10 Years Later

Anya Taylor-Joy’s film debut in Robert Eggers’ The Witch may have given the actor a cult following, but it was her role in M. Night Shyamalan’s Split in 2016 that made her a household name. A year after she shocked horror fans as Thomasin, she took on an incredibly different role in the thriller. A return to form for Shyamalan, Split takes on the complex issue of DID. Dissociative Identity Disorder is at the crux of the movie as James McAvoy takes on 24 separate identities in his role of Kevin.

Viewers only get to see some of them, but his immense talent in showing just a few is one of the best examples of character work. Even more impressive is Taylor-Joy, who stands toe to toe with the performer in her role as Casey Cooke. One day when Casey is out at a birthday party, she and acquaintances Marcia (Jessica Sula) and Claire (Haley Lu Richardson) are abducted by some of Kevin’s most insidious personalities. In the locked room drama, Casey weaponizes her wits and her own experience with trauma to escape her captivity and save her life.

M. Night Shyamalan features have typically been divisive in recent years, and Split is no different. In the movie, the director posits that DID can present itself not just in personality changes, but with physical characteristics as well. One of the most notorious of these personalities, the Beast, has more muscle definition and becomes literally bigger than the other personalities. This may be controversial with the mental health community, but there is no denying that this offers a fascinating new perspective on the subject of trauma.

Kevin materialized these personalities as a response to his overbearing and abusive mother. His foil in the film is Casey, played by Anya Taylor-Joy. Immediately, it is clear that Casey has a superpower that the other abductees do not. Slowly throughout the film, Casey’s own abuse and trauma are revealed, which allows her to empathize with Kevin. While Marcia and Claire want to break their way out by force, Casey understands that the best way to escape is through intelligence and subtlety.

This is a difficult balance to maintain, but Taylor-Joy does it almost effortlessly. She establishes this in the abduction scene as it slowly dawns on Casey that there is no escape. When Kevin’s personality, Dennis, enters the girls’ car, he subdues the other two easily in the backseat. Casey, who is in the front, immediately understands the danger in this encounter. As a single tear rolls down her face, she knows that there is no point in fighting and is taken as well.

What could be considered weakness or a fault in her character is exactly the opposite. Casey knows that she is a survivor. She has endured one monster before and will find a way to survive this one as well. Casey is characterized by her creativity in finding a way out of horrifying situations, which aids her until the very end of the movie. Just like in The Witch, Taylor-Joy accepts the task of a difficult character that could be misunderstood and instead makes it iconic. In the decade since Split first premiered, no other character has quite reached the heights of this one.

#3366. This Apple Watch Is a Lifehacker 'Gift of the Year' Award Winner, and It's $50 Off During Black Friday

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and users who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

The majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

#3364. 5-Episode Netflix Thriller Series Adapts One Of Harlan Coben's First Novels

While Harlan Coben had penned a handful of Myron Bolitar novels before writing the book that Netflix adapted into a show in 2021, the series was based on one of his first standalone novels. If Prime Video’s Reacher franchise proves one thing, it is that streaming fans love a good page-to-screen adaptation. To be more specific, streaming show adaptations of best-selling crime, thriller, and mystery novels tend to fare extraordinarily well on Prime Video, Netflix, Hulu, and Peacock alike.

Whether it is an adaptation of Andrea Mara’s novel All Her Fault breaking viewing records on Peacock or Netflix’s 30-episode take on Matthew Quick’s book The Night Agent rivaling Reacher in its popularity, the formula has proven a hit over and over again. Recently, Prime Video’s Cross cashed in on this trend, although the streaming service’s 2014 hit Bosch and its many spinoffs pioneered the approach over a decade earlier.

However, the legendary crime writer Harlan Coben is something of an unusual case when it comes to streaming shows. Coben first became a bestselling author back in 1990 with his standalone novel Play Dead, followed, by 1991’s Miracle Cure. However, it was the 12-book Myron Bolitar series that made Coben a star, beginning with 1995’s Deal Breaker. Despite the popularity of this novel series, Netflix has mostly adapted his standalone books, like Gone for Good, to the screen rather than Myron Bolitar novels.

Related in 2002, Gone for Good was a major hit for Coben. The novel follows Will, who is horrified to learn the disturbing truth about his brother Ken’s disappearance eleven years earlier after his girlfriend goes missing in the present day. Released in August 2021, Gone for Good’s Netflix adaptation relocated the story to France and changed some names accordingly, starring Finnegan Oldfield as Guillaume and Nicolas Duvauchelle as his missing brother, Fred.

Unlike Prime Video’s Reacher franchise, Netflix’s Coben adaptations all feature different main characters in stories that have no canon connections. Even though there are plenty of Myron Bolitar books to adapt, and many more YA spinoff novels starring his nephew Mickey, the streaming service has thus far opted to focus instead on Coben’s standalone efforts. These include No Second Chance, The Stranger, The Innocent, The Woods, Gone For Good, Stay Close, Hold Tight, Fool Me Once, Missing You, Run Away, and I Will Always Find You.

If that list seems long, that’s because it is. All told, there are 13 Coben shows on Netflix, with seven being English-language productions, while a further six are foreign-language shows like Gone For Good. Interestingly enough, much like Michael Connelly’s The Lincoln Lawyer was a Matthew McConaughey movie before the novel series became a Netflix show, the first screen adaptation of Coben’s work was a feature length movie, director Guillame Canet’s 2006 thriller Tell No One.

If the fact that Tell No One and Gone For Good are French-language productions didn’t give it away, Coben’s work has a massive worldwide fan base that spans the globe. His twisty thrillers translate well into other languages, which is why The Woods, Just One Look, and Hold Tight were Polish productions, The Innocent is a Spanish series, and 2025’s Caught hailed from Argentina.

Between that Coben series and the same year’s long-awaited comic adaptation The Eternaut, Argentina is emerging as a major hub for Netflix shows. However, it is tough to beat some of the writer’s earliest shows. With its clever twists, inventive plotting, and poignant character work, Netflix’s 2021 hit Gone For Good remains one of the author’s most underrated adaptations to date.

#3360. 33 Years Later, the Coldest Quote in Action Thriller History Still Hits Hard

The Fugitive took the world by storm when it was released in 1993. Not only was this action-thriller film, based on the television series from the 1960s, a massive box-office success, but it was also a critical darling and, miraculously, a major Oscar contender, receiving nominations for Best Picture and a win for Tommy Lee Jones for Best Supporting Actor. Starring Harrison Ford as Dr. Richard Kimble, a man wrongfully convicted of the murder of his wife who goes on the run from U.S. Marshals, The Fugitive, directed by Andrew Davis, shares little resemblance to other movies recognized by the Academy Awards, even the other blockbusters. And that especially applies to Jones' surprising Oscar win for playing U.S. Marshal Samuel Gerard, who leads the charge in pursuit of Kimble. When voters heard Gerard's legendary line, "I don't care," one of the coldest lines in thriller movie history, they had no choice but to hand Jones the Oscar.

Harrison Ford was at the peak of his powers in the early '90s, with two iconic characters in Han Solo and Indiana Jones already under his belt. To upend his heroic status on the big screen, The Fugitive had Ford on the defensive, running away from federal prosecution for a crime he didn't commit, but who can really be sure that he didn't slay his wife? Operating on the opposite side of the law and serving out justice is Tommy Lee Jones as the unflappable Samuel Gerard, who unconventionally has his big showdown with Kimble during the film's first act inside a storm drain. Obtaining a lost gun, Richard Kimble has Gerard in his crosshairs, but rather than shooting, he, once again, insists that he didn't kill his wife, to which Gerard, holding his hands in the air in compliance, responds, "I don't care!" These three words immediately entered the Hollywood canon.

Jones, the consummate professional who has consistently carried a no-nonsense, unfussy attitude to the screen, perfectly distills his persona with The Fugitive's most biting line of dialogue. It may not be a quippy retort or badass affirmation, but Gerard laid down the law and outlined the harsh reality of Kimble's predicament while being confronted at gunpoint by a potentially violent fugitive. Most movies provide their law enforcement officers with an altruistic motive, complemented by a flowery speech about the moral importance of the law, but The Fugitive underlines that being a sworn officer is just a job. It is not in Gerard's job description to be the judge and jury of Kimble's murder case, and his opinion is irrelevant, even if he believed his innocence. The line is a sobering punch in the face for Kimble, whose profession as a doctor relies on giving opinions and persuading clients.

It's the rare callback line that doesn't deserve an eye roll.

The Fugitive is a truly timeless film. Its rich simplicity, tight narrative and genre construction felt like a throwback to Golden Age Hollywood, which likely appealed to members of the Academy Awards. With two towering stars, a compelling premise, and a balanced confection of spectacle and character, The Fugitive, which later received an unnecessary sequel, U.S. Marshals, makes the art of filmmaking look easy, as it nails the fundamentals of narrative storytelling with ease. The moment that even the stuffiest Oscar voters had to put their hands up and give Tommy Lee Jones the statuette had to have been the "I don't care" scene in the storm drain, as the Men in Black actor delivered the fury of a Shakespeare monologue in just three one-syllable words. There's something so undeniable about Jones' conviction as his character faces a crossroads. A desperate Kimble could feasibly pull the trigger, and Gerard shows fear, but he never lets it interfere with his devout commitment to his job.

Speaking to the movie's timeless nature, "I don't care" is a moment that could have emerged in a Warner Bros. thriller from the 1940s. The brevity of the line is not its only admirable feat, as Tommy Lee Jones' signature moment in The Fugitive crystallizes the dramatic weight of the film. Andrew Davis' enduring thriller is devoid of themes and subtext in the traditional sense because it's a film about characters defined by their actions. Samuel Gerard has nothing of deep substance to say to Kimble during this pivotal moment. He just wants to bring this man into custody. When you're stuck in a grave misunderstanding, arguing with someone defined by their profession is an impossible mountain to climb.

As live TV service integration becomes a bigger feature in streaming devices, we look at how these sticks and boxes can place your favorites within closer reach.

After that, it's onto the extra features, like gaming, voice search and screen mirroring. These factors don't weigh quite as heavily toward the final score, but they're nice to have if they work well, and extremely distracting if they don't.

The main reason to get a streaming stick is that your TV is either missing a feature you want, or you'd rather not replace a perfectly good television just because it doesn't connect to the internet and download apps.

These are both great reasons to invest in these small and relatively inexpensive devices. After all, even the best TVs under $500 are still a strain on your bank balance, and if there's nothing wrong with your existing set, why send it out to the trash when you don't need to?

Or if you want to go the other way, I'd advise the Apple TV 4K — not because it doesn't have AI (the 2026 box has the new AI Siri experience), but because it's not that interesting, so you won't ever feel compelled to use it. I'm being a little unfair; it works with Apple's own services, but it's less reliable for third-party apps and services.

#3357. iOS 27 gave your iPhone an alarm feature that’s long been missing

Alarms are one of the most important iPhone features, and iOS 27 offers a key feature that should help your alarm actually wake you: a new volume setting for alarms that’s independent of other volume settings.

Have you ever accidentally slept through an alarm? We’ve all done it. And most often for me, it’s because my alarm volume was unintentionally set to a very low level.

I suspect that’s a pretty common reason for missed alarms. And in iOS 27, Apple finally has the fix—but it requires manually setting up.

Inside Settings ⇾ Sounds & Haptics, you can now set a volume for alarms that’s independent from the systemwide ringtone setting.

iOS 27 has two new sections in this Settings screen: Alarms and Timers, and Alerts and System Sounds. Both include ‘Match Ringtone Volume’ toggles that are on by default. This means your volume for alarms, timers, alerts, and other system sounds are all determined by the ringtone volume.

But if you disable the Alarms and Timers toggle, you’ll get a new volume slider that applies only to those system functions, and won’t be impacted by your ringtone volume.

As seen above, this means you can crank the Alarms and Timers volume up to the maximum level without making every other system sound, including notifications and phone calls, be similarly deafening.

So the next time you sleep through your alarm, it won’t be because the alarm was too quiet.

In case you missed it, iOS 26 introduced a welcome feature that lets you set custom snooze durations for alarms, and also an option to have alarms trigger on your iPhone even if you’re wearing an Apple Watch.

Do you plan to set a custom volume setting for alarms in iOS 27? Let us know in the comments.
