#3353. 7 Masterpiece Christmas Books Better Than ‘A Christmas Carol’

Beatriz (Bea) Valero de Urquia is a Books & Literature author at Collider, where she focuses on Lists surrounding recent bestsellers, classical novels, and everything in between. She is a historian by training and a bilingual reader, moving between English and Spanish literature.   Beatriz began her career as a technology writer at a startup in the UK. Almost a decade later, journalism has taken her to five cities across three continents and into business reporting, cultural criticism, and live TV commentary. She joined Collider in 2026.  Beatriz has a passion for travelling and loves keeping an eye on the books headed to the screen. One of her favorite pastimes is critiquing the historical accuracy of period movies. She also once volunteered for the Charles Dickens Museum. Beatriz also has a core belief that a book is always better than the movie, but she has been happy to have been proven wrong in a couple of occasions.

When she isn’t reading, Beatriz is watching musicals, stage managing Shakespeare plays with a local theater group or doing historical research. She enjoys tracing family trees for her history and genealogy TikTok, creating databases for historical analysis and sifting through 17th-century stories for the novel she is currently in the process of writing.

Every Christmas, we turn to the same stories. The same movies the grandparents like, and the song that plays every single Christmas Eve so that everyone in the family can sing along. It is comforting to have stories to return to. Many of the traditions we return to were actually cemented by none other than Charles Dickens. A Christmas Carol is the most popular, having been adapted hundreds of times. Dickens cemented Christmas as we know it today, but that doesn't mean there aren't other Christmas stories worth knowing.

A Christmas story can be a Christmas story for many reasons. The setting, for instance, sets the mood, but the values are what stay. During this time of year, it is normal to gravitate toward stories with deeper meaning that reflect on what one is grateful for. Some books have achieved this with incredible mastery. Here are the best.

"'Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents,' grumbled Jo, lying on the rug." Louisa May Alcott's Little Women might not be everyone's go-to Christmas story, but it should be. The word "Christmas" appears twice in the first sentence of the book and, within the first couple chapters, the March sisters have already given away their Christmas breakfast to a hungry family. It is something out of a Dickens story.

The original Little Women volume, not including its continuations, takes place over a year, bookended by two very different Christmases. During this time, Alcott subtly shows the importance of maintaining the values we so cherish during the festive season year-round. Marmee often encourages her daughters to be selfless, humble, studious, and caring. By the end of this volume, Beth is recovering from scarlet fever and the sisters receive the best present they could have wished for: their father's return. The book is perfect for the holiday season.

Claire Keegan's novella Small Things like These is quietly heartbreaking. Set in Ireland in 1985, it follows Bill Furlong, a coal and fuel merchant. The week before Christmas, he goes about his routine while thinking about what presents to get his wife and daughters. One day, he visits a local convent and is surprised to find a young woman named Sarah locked in a nearby shed and asking about a baby. He frees her and leaves her with the Mother Superior, who says she was playing a game. The girl reminds Bill of his mother, who was an unmarried teenager when she got pregnant with him. Over the following days, Bill cannot shake the suspicion that something terrible is going on in the convent.

This story shows that Christmas stories do not need to be wrapped in a pretty bow. It is also possible to read something themed to the season that deals with ethical questions. In the case of Small Things like These, Keegan discusses the difficult topic of Ireland's Magdalene laundries, where young women were imprisoned and forced to do labor. The subject is treated with the dignity and care it deserves, showing how a single person can choose to do what is right in the face of larger injustices, even when the cost is high.

Hogfather is missing. The Auditors of Reality, a group of celestial bureaucrats, have hired the assassin Mr. Teatime to murder Discworld’s Santa Claus equivalent, who gives children presents on the night of Hogswatch, on December 32nd. Without children's belief in Hogfather, the sun won't rise. The only one who understands the importance of Hogfather's role is Death, and so he must step in. Aided by Albert, his reluctant pixie servant, Death puts on a red suit and starts delivering presents. His granddaughter, Susan, is tasked with traveling to the Tooth Fairy's realm to bring Hogfather back.

As funny and magical as all of Terry Pratchett's stories, Hogfather is a wonderful seasonal read. In addition to an incredible display of whimsy, the book includes one of the most thoughtful discussions of the importance of faith and why we go to such great lengths to keep the magic of the holidays alive. "Humans need fantasy to be human," Death tells Susan. "To be the place where the falling angel meets the rising ape."

After Dickens, Russian composer Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky has a monopoly on Christmas. However, not many people know that the Nutcracker ballet, often performed during the holiday season, is based on Alexandre Dumas' story, which is itself an adaptation of an older (and much darker) short story: The Nutcracker and the Mouse King by E. T. A. Hoffmann.

One Christmas Eve (of course), Marie notices a nutcracker under the tree. That evening, while playing with the nutcracker, she sees mice start to come out from beneath the floor. Their leader seems to be a seven-headed Mouse King, taller than all the others. Suddenly, all of Marie's toys come to life and, led by the nutcracker, begin to fight the mouse army. They are at a disadvantage, so Marie throws her slipper at the Mouse King to stop him from capturing the nutcracker. The morning after, Marie wakes up with a bandaged arm and no idea if the events she witnessed were real. The only person who believes her is her godfather, who then tells her the tragic story of Princess Pirlipat and Madam Mouserinks, the Queen of the Mice, which explains the origins of nutcrackers.

Yes, this story was written by the same author who wrote both Breakfast at Tiffany's and In Cold Blood. And yes, it is a perfect Christmas classic. Truman Capote's "A Christmas Memory" is set in rural Alabama in the 1930s. It was inspired by Capote's own life and his experience of the holiday season in a family with financial difficulties. The short story is beautiful, warm, funny, and deep. It will also absolutely break your heart.

“It's fruitcake weather!” Buddy's elderly cousin announces, declaring the start of winter. The relationship between the seven-year-old boy and his cousin is the heart of Capote's story. They are two childlike, wide-eyed people in a stern and strict family. During the story, they gather the ingredients to make fruitcakes and share them with friends. Years later, Buddy looks back at the simple magic of those shared Christmases. The prose is as beautiful as the story, and it is worth reading, if only for the last few lines. The cousin character is said to have been inspired by Sook, a relative the author lived with as a boy, who may have had intellectual disabilities. Capote called her "a genius."

The plot of this story is as simple as most people's holiday celebrations. Dubliner Gabriel Conroy is a teacher and part-time book reviewer. One winter evening, he attends a party with his wife, Gretta, hosted by family members. There is music, pudding, a goose, and tipsy guests. While greeting friends and old acquaintances, Gabriel thinks of the speech he has to give. At the end of the evening, a guest sings a sorrowful song. Gretta is moved by the song, and later confesses it reminds her of a young man she once loved who has passed away. Gabriel could be anyone. What makes him stand out is the beautifully crafted way he thinks about life and death.

"The Dead" closes James Joyce's Dubliners. At almost 16,000 words, it can also be a short novella. Whatever its definition, the story is timeless and deeply moving. It discusses local topics related to Irishness, while reflecting on universal themes such as love and loss. The ending, "His soul swooned slowly as he heard the snow falling faintly through the universe and faintly falling, like the descent of their last end, upon all the living and the dead," might be one of the most beautiful and poignant lines in the history of literature.

What is a 14th-century Middle English chivalric romance doing in a list of Christmas books? Well, it is a great story, and it is set at Christmastime, so it meets every requirement to be here. A warning: it is written in alliterative verse, so it might be denser than other picks, although J. R. R. Tolkien himself has an accessible translation. Still, it is absolutely worth the effort. And what better way to end the year's reading challenge than with a classic?

Sir Gawain and the Green Knight takes place in King Arthur's court during the celebrations between Christmas and New Year. Suddenly, a giant green knight interrupts the feast. He offers his axe to any man who dares to strike him. However, in return, that person will agree to take a blow in a year and a day. Sir Gawain, one of King Arthur's knights, accepts and beheads him. A year later, on the way to that appointment, Gawain is taken in by a generous lord and his wife. What follows is a game of temptation and a test of honor that Gawain must pass.

Samsung's Dolby Atmos soundbars are also discounted by as much as $400, while Bose and LG have more affordable options for anyone looking to improve dialogue clarity, add some bass, or enjoy surround sound without a complicated setup. Whether you're shopping for a compact speaker for a bedroom TV or a more immersive system for movie nights, here are the deals worth considering.

For anyone building a premium home theater around a large TV, the Sony Bravia Theater Trio is down to $1,498 from $2,199.99, saving you $701.99, or roughly 32%. Unlike a conventional soundbar, the Trio uses three separate front speakers for the left, center, and right channels, helping spread dialogue and effects across a wider soundstage. You can read PCMag’s “excellent” review for more details.

The Sony Bravia Theater Bar 7 is down to $718 from $869 for anyone who wants a single soundbar under the TV. Its nine speakers include upward- and side-firing drivers that widen the soundstage and give Dolby Atmos some height, but there’s no subwoofer, so the now $898 Bar 7 with a wireless sub bundle (down from $1,099.99) might be the better pick for deeper bass.

Moving down Sony's lineup, the Bravia Theater Bar 6 is $548, down from $699.99, and pairs a 3.1.2-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer and upward-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos height effects. Spending $100 more gets you the Bravia Theater System 6, now $648 from $799.99, which adds rear speakers in a 5.1-channel setup for movies and games where sound moves behind you.

For a more affordable upgrade, the Sony Bravia Theater Bar 5 is down to $278 from $349.99, saving you nearly $72. It's a 3.1-channel system with a dedicated center speaker and wireless subwoofer, so dialogue should come through more clearly while music and movie effects get some additional low-end presence.

Sony’s older systems are discounted too, including the HT-S400 at $258, down from $299, which pairs a 2.1-channel soundbar and wireless subwoofer with S-Force Pro Front Surround to widen the sound for everyday TV, sports, and casual movies. The HT-S40R is arguably the better deal at the same $258, down from $329.99, since it adds two rear speakers for a full 5.1-channel setup, though neither model supports Dolby Atmos.

For smaller rooms or for anyone who mainly wants dialogue to come across more clearly, Bose has two compact soundbars on sale: The newer Bose TV Speaker (2nd Gen) is down to $239 from $299, with an updated acoustic design that Bose says improves clarity and overall sound performance. Meanwhile, the original Bose TV Speaker is $199, down from $279, and offers a similarly compact design with a dedicated dialogue mode and adjustable bass.

Samsung’s HW-Q800H is down to $697.99 from $1,097.99, a $400 cut on a 5.1.2-channel Dolby Atmos soundbar with a wireless subwoofer. Its side- and upward-firing speakers help place effects around and above you, while a dedicated center channel keeps dialogue clear during busy action scenes.

For something that takes up less space, the Samsung HW-S60D is $277.99, down from $399.99, and fits seven speakers, including side-firing drivers, into a compact 5.0-channel soundbar. It also supports Dolby Atmos, Adaptive Sound, and a voice enhancement mode, along with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, AirPlay, and Chromecast for music streaming. That said, it has no upward-firing speakers or subwoofer, so its height effects and bass won’t match that of the Q800H.

If you're looking for a complete surround sound system without spending several hundred dollars, the LG S6FTR is down to $249.99 from $399.99, saving you $150, or roughly 38%. It's a 5.1-channel home theater package with a soundbar, subwoofer, and dedicated rear speakers. That makes it particularly appealing for action movies and games, where directional sound adds to the experience.

The LG S40TR is another affordable option for anyone who wants rear speakers included in the box. It's currently $199.99, down from $279.99, and offers a 4.1-channel arrangement with a wireless subwoofer and two rear speakers. This should give movie soundtracks a greater sense of direction than a basic soundbar, while the subwoofer handles the lower frequencies that smaller TV speakers often struggle to reproduce.

At just under $187, the S60T is the least expensive system in this roundup, pairing a 3.1-channel soundbar with a wireless subwoofer for clearer dialogue and fuller sound than your TV’s speakers. That said, it lacks rear speakers and Dolby Atmos height channels, so it’s better suited to someone who wants a simple, affordable upgrade without filling the room with additional hardware.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

#3351. MagSafe Monday: Anker’s MagGo Pro 2 has a built-in fan to keep 25W Qi2.2 charging from slowing down

The biggest issue with Qi 2.2 on MagSafe batteries is the slowdown caused by heat. It doesn’t matter if the battery specs say it can charge at Qi2.2 speeds if the heat slows it down after 15 minutes. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro directly targets heat with a built-in fan in the MagSafe battery.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Heat is the enemy of MagSafe charging, which is why it slows to a crawl on a hot day and why most MagSafe batteries can’t hold their top speed for an entire charge. Anker’s answer in the MagGo 2 Pro is a small fan inside of it. Anker says it keeps the charging surface below 96.8°F, and the fan adjusts its speed based on what’s plugged in and how the charge is progressing. You can switch between Cool and Silent modes if you don’t want to hear it running at all.

The result of having this fan is a Qi2.2 power bank that actually reaches Qi2.2 speeds for a full charge. Anker rates it at 25% on an iPhone 17 Pro in 10 minutes, then to 50% in 25 minutes, which is the kind of speed you’d normally expect from a wired charging session.

The MagGo 2 Pro battery is 10,000mAh, which is enough for a little over one full charge of an iPhone Pro Max and closer to two on a standard iPhone. Size-wise, it has about the same footprint as the iPhone itself and is roughly an ounce lighter than Anker’s standard MagGo. It’s not a slim battery, but for one with a fan, it’s workable in your travel bag, crossbody, etc.

The single USB-C port works both directions at up to 45 watts. If you plug in a 45-watt charger to it, the MagGo 2 Pro can charge from empty to 80% in under an hour. The same port will charge a Mac or an iPad up to 45 watts in a pinch, which is a nice add-on for a MagSafe battery. You are not going to charge up your MacBook Pro from zero to full with it, but it’s a nice way to get a little charge in an emergency at the airport, etc.

One thing to know before you buy: the cable in the box is a 1-foot USB-C-to-USB-C cable, and Anker says that reaching the full 45-watt recharge speed requires a 45-watt-rated cable. So keep that in mind as you pack for a trip.

Anker put a small display on the side that cycles through six screens with a side button: charging wattage, battery percentage, battery health, and temperature. It’s a nice touch to know you are reaching the 25-watt Qi 2.2 speed.

There’s also a built-in stand that adjusts from flat to 80 degrees and folds back into the body when you’re done. You can also quickly turn off charging if you simply want to use it as a stand. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro comes in Phantom Gray, Burgundy Red, Polar Night Blue, and Starlight Silver.

Qi2.2 is the Holy Grail of MagSafe chargers, but as I said in the beginning, it’s irrelevant if the heat throttles it. To get full 25-watt MagSafe charging on the go, you’ll likely need something with a fan, unless you’re in colder weather. The Anker MagGo 2 Pro solves that problem with a built-in fan, a handy side display, and a stand.

The Anker MagGo 2 Pro is available on Amazon and directly from Anker.

The best smartwatch is almost always the one that works with your phone. Over the past few years, brands have moved away from universal compatibility and toward platform-specific watches that will only work if you use a particular phone.

One of the remaining holdouts is Amazfit, which launched the excellent Active 3 Premium that works on iPhone and Android. It's half the price of Apple or Google's watches, but you wouldn't know it from its impressive fitness tracking features.

It's incredible value, but if you're looking for the closest integration you can get with your phone or smart features like emergency or health alerts, then I'd recommend the Apple Watch Series 12 (iPhone) or Google Pixel Watch 5 (Android) right now.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The Amazfit Active 3 Premium is the smartwatch I recommend for most people, and not just because it works with whichever phone you have. It's a fantastic fitness-tracking watch that easily holds its own against the Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5, without locking you to a specific platform or phone.

It is also incredible value — coming in at around half the price of the two flagship watches — and all the features are free with no subscription (unless you need Zepp Aura, the sleep-focused AI wellness app that generates audio to relax you). It has offline maps, tracks more than 170 activities, and comes with built-in GPS.

It has a smaller footprint (wristprint?) than many other smartwatches, with a 1.3-inch display, compared to the 1.77- or 1.96-inch Apple Watch Series 12. It's not a huge amount on paper, but it makes a big difference, as it felt smaller and less noticeable on our wrist. It's a shame it doesn't come in a few more vibrant colors, though.

While you don't get the smarts of Apple and Google's watches (emergency alerts, on-watch calls, third-party apps), fitness and activity tracking is where the Active 3 Premium really shines, with metrics to rival the best Garmin watches, like heart rate, blood oxygen, stress levels, cycle tracking, sleep quality and skin temperature.

The data all syncs to your phone, and you can view it and get insights in the Zepp app, available for Android and iPhone. If you ever used a Fitbit before the Google takeover, the Zepp app is the closest thing to that now-gone experience; easy to understand, straightforward to use, and guides you through all the different metrics.

This is particularly helpful if you're just getting into running, as the running features on the Active 3 Premium are almost as detailed as those you'd find on Garmin watches, yet everything is explained clearly, even for more complex topics like your lactate threshold and ground contact time, which assess how your foot strikes the floor.

Amazfit says that the Active 3 Premium should last 12 days between charges. Like most other smartwatches, that doesn't work out in the real world; we found that it'd generally last just over a week or eight days. That's down a bit on the spec, but still miles ahead of the 24-hour battery life on the Apple Watch Series 12.

Apple, Google and Samsung refresh their watches every year. Normally, these are pretty small upgrades, so I often recommend buying the previous year's model. But not with the Apple Watch Series 12. For the first time in almost half a decade, Apple has given the watch a pretty big health-tracking update.

The most significant change is that there's a new, more accurate heart rate sensor. This powers a few other changes, like the Readiness score you can get each day. This is something imported from other running watches and is a measure of how you've recovered after activity and how to improve the score.

I've tested watches with this kind of score and haven't found it that informative, but I know our resident runners find it particularly helpful when training for races. The improved sensors also allow for continuous heart rate monitoring (ie all day), which was previously limited to just during tracked workouts.

These practical and useful changes were only part of the Series 12 pitch. Apple also rolled out new AI Siri and a selection of 'helpful' AI-powered features, called Audio Intelligence. There are two (Live Rewind, Siri Recap), but both use the watch to capture speech around you and turn it into some form of recap.

Live Rewind is arguably the least helpful and most invasive. It listens to conversations (privately on your phone) and allows you to rewind live conversations in case you miss a detail, like someone's name (in case you were unaware you could ask the person to repeat what they said). Recap uses AI to summarize all that data into a journal-like, 'here's what happened today' note.

Honestly, these seem like gimmicks to me that very few people will ever use, and it normalizes surveillance. So, in case it wasn't clear, I wouldn't buy the watch for these and would jump into the settings to disable them. But in all other aspects, the Series 12 is the best Apple Watch you can buy right now and a worthy upgrade.

As with the Apple Watch, I wouldn't normally recommend the most recent version of the Google Pixel Watch, but this time I do think the Google Pixel Watch 5 is the better choice than the 4, but mostly because it's hard to find a new edition of the Pixel Watch 4 now that the Pixel Watch 5 exists.

That doesn't mean I don't think the Pixel Watch 5 is a great smartwatch — it is — but it's a relatively modest update this time around. But what you get for your money still makes it the best smartwatch for Android phones, especially if you own a Pixel device. And like Apple, it's the new health and safety features that are the headline.

The Pixel Watch 5 includes Breathing Emergency Detection, which is a lot like 2024's Loss of Pulse Detection, which uses the watch's sensor data to look for signs of a breathing emergency and automatically requests 911 support or trusted contacts for help. These two, along with Fall/Crash Detection, Blood Pressure Trends, and Insulin Resistance Trends, form part of Google's new "Health Guardian" suite.

Technologically, it's impressive. But do I recommend you buy the watch for them? I don't think so. It's a reassuring fallback if you do have an emergency, but you can't say with certainty that they'll always work as intended when you need them to. And reviewers (including us) can't really test them to check either.

What I like about the Pixel Watch range is that Google doesn't tie too many features exclusively to Pixel phones. The Pixel-exclusive features on the Watch 5 are: call screening, secure phone unlock, contact cards when someone calls you, and the ability to use your watch as a remote viewfinder for your phone's camera app.

The newest watch has also retained my favorite feature: repairable screens and replaceable batteries. This isn't as easy as popping the back off, but it makes the Pixel Watch 5 the most repairable smartwatch you can buy right now. iFixit even rated it a near-perfect 9/10 for repairability, while the Apple Watch Series 12 scored just 4/10.

It's not easy for me to praise Google (have you seen the Google Graveyard?), but it's a hugely positive move that saves you money in the long run and prevents otherwise good watches from going to the trash. But much of this was also true of the Pixel Watch 4, so if you can find a good deal on the older model, I'd go for that.

If you're after the best smartwatch for your phone, the three models I recommend above are going to cover most use cases, whichever phone you have. But there are a lot more smartwatches around right now.

Not every model can be the best, but some come pretty close. If you need a few more options, these are the smartwatches I still think are worth your money, and may fill a need we didn't cover in the wearables from Amazfit, Apple or Google.

Last year's Apple Watch Series 11 is so close to the older Series 10 that it does make you wonder why Apple released it, but for the first time in many years, there was a bump in battery life from 18 hours on the Series 10 to 24 hours on the Series 11. If you can get a good discount, it's a great option, but the Series 12 is a much better watch for not much more.

Read our full Apple Watch Series 11 review

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 generates free wellbeing insights from your data. This is a neat upside, as many other brands charge for this. The (potential) downside is that you need a Samsung phone to access them all in the Samsung Health app. But it's more expensive than the Galaxy Watch 8, despite modest changes and the same display. The Pixel Watch 5 is a better option unless you really need the Samsung integration.

Read our full Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 review

Apple didn't release a new budget watch in 2026, so the most recent is the 2025 SE 3. It's an excellent choice and has almost all the same features as the Series 10 and 11, minus some health-specific ones like ECG and blood oxygen monitoring. And like those models, it lacks the upgraded health sensors of the Series 12. If you can do without them, the SE 3 is a great value Apple Watch.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a useful update from the Ultra 3 with a redesigned, more accurate health sensor array and better battery life. It also comes with the same AI gimmicks as the Series 12. It's a good option if you need a larger, longer-lasting Apple Watch, but for most people, the Series 12 is the better (and cheaper) choice.

The Withings ScanWatch Light is a stripped-back version of the hybrid ScanWatch 2 I wear every day. It doesn't have a large color screen and is missing features like calls and apps, but it can track your activity, heart rate and workouts. I love the ScanWatch 2, and the compromise to reduce the cost is that the Light drops the flagship watch's health features, like an ECG. Otherwise, this is an excellent fitness tracking watch that'll last several weeks between charges.

Read our full Withings ScanWatch Light review

The CMF Watch 3 Pro is impressively cheap, retailing for less than most fitness trackers. It has a color display and two weeks of battery life; incredible at this price. But we found that step counts are inaccurate and the sleep tracking is unreliable. So I'd recommend the Amazfit Active 3 Premium instead.

Read our full Nothing CMF Watch 3 Pro review

We reviewed the first Apple Watch more than a decade ago, and we've been testing the best smartwatches ever since. The devices have gotten more complex, last longer and have way more features now, but the core of our testing has remained the same: we wear the watches, just as you would, to see how they hold up in the real world.

We look at how easy it is to set up, whether it has compatibility issues with specific phones and spending hours poking around in the software, looking for settings, apps and other features that make the device worth your money. Over the years, these watches have transitioned from phone companions to health and wellbeing trackers.

So we also focus on how these tools work, whether the tracking is accurate, how it compares to the competition and whether there's value in measuring what the company says you should. We wear the best smartwatches out on runs, during workouts, while sleeping and going about our day to see how they cope.

Over the past few years, brands have added more safety features to their watches, like irregular heartbeat notifications, sleep apnea alerts, crash and fall detection and hypertension alerts. These are things we can't practically test, so we can't verify that these work as intended or described.

In the U.S., health features are regulated by the FDA, so there is some degree of verification, but because we can't check that ourselves, I wouldn't recommend that you buy any of these watches specifically for these safety features. At the very least, they should be secondary to some other safety check.

It's not something you can predict, but sometimes a health issue does come along when you're testing a smartwatch. This happened to one of our writers — her Garmin watch alerted her to a potential heart problem she didn't know about, and that prompted her to go to the hospital to get checked out.

Before you go too far into your journey for a new smartwatch, first you need to work out which ones will work with your phone. The Apple Watch only works with iPhones, and some Android-focused watches have features that are exclusive to specific phones (I'm thinking of offerings from Google and Samsung here).

There are plenty of options that'll work with both platforms, but they generally aren't the flagship models that get a lot of attention every summer and fall, like the watch I rate as the best smartwatch right now, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium. It's more of a fitness smartwatch, but it can do a lot of what the others can do for a lot less.

And that's one of the other big choices you have to make: do you want a fitness watch that has smartwatch features, or a smartwatch as a companion to your phone that can track your fitness? These sound similar — and they are — but the difference is how much of the focus is put on either the smartwatch or fitness features.

Fitness smartwatches evolved from the best fitness trackers, with larger displays and more sensors. The best smartwatches started life as Bluetooth-connected extensions of your phone and over time became devices that keep you connected to your digital life, even when you're away from your phone working out.

The Apple Watch Series 12 and Google Pixel Watch 5 are the best compromise between the two, but there are plenty of other options in our Also Consider section that also straddle that line or lean one way or the other. Though, if you need a cellular connection in your watch, those are pretty much limited to the flagship models.

#3347. Ridley Scott’s 116-Minute Sci-Fi Masterpiece 'Alien' Is the Perfect Watch Before It’s Cut From Netflix

If you need any convincing as to why Ridley Scott is held in such high regard by movie fans, you only need to fire up Netflix before November 30 and catch his classic Alien. The pioneering sci-fi horror movie led to a franchise consisting of seven films, two spin-offs, and the TV hit Alien: Earth. However, back in 1979, it was just Scott’s vision that terrified audiences and changed the genre as we know it, with star Sigourney Weaver becoming an icon for the ages. If you’ve never experienced the nail-biting first chapter of the space saga, now is the time.

Set in the year 2122, the film takes place in a future where galactic space travel is not only possible, it’s industrialized. Commercial towing craft Nostromo is diverted to a planetoid, answering a distress signal from an alien spacecraft. Once there, an alien attaches itself to one of the crew without his knowledge, only to burst out of him once he's back on board. Escaping to the dark corridors of the ship, the alien (known as a Xenomorph) grows rapidly and starts hunting down the crew members one by one. Only Ellen Ripley (Weaver), who had reservations about the diversion in the first place, stands a chance of outwitting this terrifying new foe.

Scott conceived of the idea after the success of Star Wars, bringing his own brand of intensity to deep space and making a star of Weaver, who was appearing in her first starring role and just her third movie appearance. Nearly 50 years after its release, it’s still considered a pivotal moment in the sci-fi genre and film in general, thanks to the risks it took with well-known formulas.

The movies you finish at one in the morning.

Prior to Scott’s film, the idea of space travel was mostly aspirational for Hollywood studios. Star Trek invited us to “boldly go where no man has gone before,” Star Wars offered swashbuckling adventures, and a decade on from the Apollo 11 moon landing, space seemed like a frontier. What Alien did was introduce the idea of space as a void, a lonely stretch of isolation where its inhabitants were alone in the truest sense. Scott took that concept and used it as the basis for a classic “haunted house” horror tale, teasing theater patrons with the poster’s tagline: “In space, no one can hear you scream.”

It also broke barriers with its visual presentation. The alien creatures and environments designed by the Swiss artist H. R. Giger looked otherworldly, inspired by surrealistic landscapes and biomechanical concepts. The spaces surrounding Ripley were foreign and unsettling, adding to the sense of being alone against this creature that has no empathy or reason, only the instinct to kill. Its influence is immeasurable – if you’ve seen a sci-fi movie where the crew of a spaceship are picked off by a deadly stowaway, it’s likely Alien’s DNA is in there. In the gaming world, titles like Halo and Doom both share the themes of the movie and its sequels. Its most impactful element, however, was its human star.

Ellen Ripley would have been an outlier in science fiction simply for being a female lead, but her influence goes beyond simple box ticking. She wasn’t like the cavalier heroes we were used to seeing flying through asteroid fields or battling little green men. In Alien, she is pragmatic, resourceful, and tough, doing what she has to do to survive without flourishes or grandstanding. She remained the key component of the first four Alien movies, and inspired a number of female sci-fi lead characters in the years since. The gritty resilience of The Terminator’s Sarah Connor, the relentlessness of Katniss Everdeen, and the strength of Mad Max hero Furiosa all owe something to Ellen Ripley, making her a key component of centering female characters in a historically male-dominated genre.

Given her influence on women in genre filmmaking, it’s surprising that the character was originally written as male, with no dialogue changing when the gender was flipped. Speaking to the American Film Institute in 2009, Weaver pointed out this as what attracted her to the part. “It was a character written as a man, so it was written in a very straightforward way,” she said. “She’s a direct person, who didn’t suddenly have these scenes where she was vulnerable. She didn’t throw up her hands and wait for someone to save her.”

Ridley Scott's Alien still holds up nearly half a century later, providing a benchmark by which all follow-ups, and sci-fi in general, are compared. The simplicity of the storytelling, combined with the complexity of the visual filmmaking, made for an unforgettable deep space nightmare that left everyone wondering what horrors may lie just beyond the stars.Alien is on Netflix, with November 30 as the final day to watch.

#3342. The Perfect ‘Hunger Games’ Cast if the Movie Were Made in 2026

Pop culture found its favorite love triangle when The Hunger Games was transformed into a blockbuster movie franchise. Based on the young adult novels by Suzanne Collins, the filmis set in a dystopian future in the nation of Panem and follows a teenage girl named Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), who volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised, annual fight to the death. Alongside her fellow district tribute Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson), she must survive the brutal arena while unintentionally sparking a rebellion against the oppressive Capitol.

With the highly anticipated The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping reigniting the obsession with the original, it’s time to ponder what The Hunger Games might look like if it were made in 2026. In our dream iteration, we will fill the ensemble with rising generational stars alongside legends of the craft while reflecting the nature of the characters both in the book and on screen. Though the original cast may be untouchable to some devoted fans, this list is what dreams are made of.

The Hunger Games lives and dies with Katniss Everdeen, the Girl on Fire. Tough and fiercely protective, Katniss sets the action in motion in the first film when she volunteers as tribute after her sister Primrose's (Willow Shields) name is drawn at the reaping for the 74th Hunger Games. Armed with exceptional archery skills, a sharp survival instinct, and a guarded demeanor, she enters the arena alongside fellow District 12 tribute Peeta Mellark. After her breakout Oscar-nominated role in Winter's Bone, The Hunger Games proved that Jennifer Lawrence could play a stoic, self-reliant young woman forced into a gritty, mature environment. Lawrence brought natural athleticism, quiet wariness, and ferocity without over-glamorizing the story's brutal elements.

Lawrence masterfully balanced a relatable authenticity with grounded maturity. She was a reluctant, real-world survivor who was never pretentious, carrying the high-stakes dystopian thriller by projecting real fear and compassion. One young star who masters everything that elevated Lawrence's Katniss is Sadie Sink. Showcasing her knack for portraying complex teenage heroines, Sink excels at playing a guarded young woman who conceals deep trauma and fierce loyalty beneath a tough exterior. Between Max Mayfield in Stranger Things and her recent turn as Jean Grey in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Sink is no stranger to massive franchises and is never intimidated. While the character would embark on a romantic love triangle, Sink's iteration of Katniss would be fiercely independent and self-reliant. Her ability to play raw, authentic dramatic parts, as seen on Broadway in John Proctor Is the Villain and in the film adaptation of The Whale, would add gravitas, rooting Katniss in weighted reality.

Hailing from District 12, it's Peeta Mellark. The lovelorn baker's son has harbored a long-standing crush on Katniss, so, of course, it added intrigue for viewers watching the 74th Hunger Games, as Peeta and Katniss had a star-crossed lovers' narrative built around them. Unlike other hardened competitors, Peeta used verbal skills, artistic camouflage abilities, and genuine empathy to survive. Joining Katniss in defying the Capitol's orders, Peeta emerged as a co-winner and helped spark the revolution that followed. The green-flag boy of the story, Josh Hutcherson brought authentic emotional depth and warmth to the role, making it easy to champion him. With a gentle spirit and sincerity, Hutcherson instilled a protective love and strategic charm into Peeta that was rightly earned.

Peeta served as the emotional core of The Hunger Games. To take on this part today, an actor who has the will to battle without diminishing his genuine heart and spirit is required. That actor is rising superstar Walker Scobell. Best known for starring in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Scobell would be a compelling Peeta due to his charm, sarcastic wit, and ability to balance vulnerability with fierce loyalty. Oh, and he's well-versed in action-centric storytelling. Scobell is naturally earnest and charming, which would seamlessly translate to the character. His smile is instantly disarming, though how much smile is there really when you're inside the arena? Though Scobell is a teen action hero, Peeta is defined more by his deep empathy, artistic heart, and emotional resilience. As seen in Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Scobell balances those traits through a pure tenderness. Energetic and expressive, there's a universe in which Scobell would be even more beloved than Hutcherson, and that's quite a high bar to achieve.

Young adult stories need a tinge of a love triangle, and in The Hunger Games, Gale Hawthorne filled that third slot. He is Katniss' best friend and hunting partner, and they share a similar hardscrabble life. Gale fiercely hates the Capitol and the oppressive system of the Games, questioning why anyone would watch them. He serves as the emotional support for Katniss' family while she's in the Games. In the film, Gale was played by a hunk: Liam Hemsworth. He naturally captured Gale's quiet intensity, physical stature, and silent protectiveness. His expressive presence was a means of communication. It also served as a stark contrast in stature to Hutcherson's Peeta.

Hemsworth balanced the range of emotion necessary to bring Gale to life. Playing Gale requires conveying deep loyalty, heartbreak, and quiet resolve against his underlying rage and revolutionary spark. Rather than leaning closer to a Hollywood heartthrob or Gale's physical likeness in the book, the perfect pick would be David Iacono. Tall and muscular with olive skin, dark hair, and gray eyes, Iacono fits the classic look of District 12's "Seam" neighborhood. Audiences are quite familiar with Iacono's ability to play a devoted, caring romantic interest during his time as Cam Cameron in The Summer I Turned Pretty. He excels at portraying the quiet tenderness that Gale would share with Katniss in the woods before the Games tear their lives apart. Iacono has shown he can handle darker, high-stakes crime and thriller material, as seen in Cinnamon, Grand Army, and Fresh Kills. It would give him the edge needed for Gale's eventual transformation. Following his performance in Jurassic World Rebirth, it's clear Iacono can carry heavy physical action and anchor scenes in a massive pop culture franchise.

Four of the largest communities on the planet, and four completely different reasons to belong to one. Here is yours, what it would give you, and the argument you would be having within a week.

You belong to the fandom that is really about comfort. Hogwarts works on people because it is a place rather than a plot, and the pull is not the wizard war so much as the corridors, the food, the weather and the sense that somebody is expecting you.

You belong to the deepest fandom on this list, the one where somebody has always read further than you and is quietly delighted to say so. Middle-earth rewards patience more than any other world in popular culture.

You belong to the loudest and largest tent of the four, the one where three generations are all watching the same thing and none of them agree about any of it. That disagreement is not a flaw in this fandom, it is the main activity.

You belong to the thinking fandom, the one that turns up for the argument rather than the explosion. Trek has always been a series of ethical problems in space, and the people who love it love being asked what they would have done.

With the upcoming film fleshing out the full lore and mythology of Haymitch Abernathy, it will only deepen the allure of this fascinating character. When audiences first met him, it was revealed that he was the only living person from District 12 to have ever won the Hunger Games. Because of his victor status, he is assigned to act as the cynical, hard-drinking mentor to Katniss and Peeta. Despite his vices, he used his sharp wits to help the duo win vital corporate and public sponsors, famously leading them to present themselves as star-crossed lovers. Both a logical and surprising casting choice, Woody Harrelson perfectly blended cynical humor with the genuine emotional depth of a man plagued by decades of trauma. He avoided turning him into a one-note drunken bum, giving him the right amount of preserved dignity beneath the mess.

Though he was known for his over-the-top characterizations in other signature roles, Harrelson's small glances and weary demeanor brought immense fruitfulness to Haymitch. An actor who can do the most while exuding very little, yet serve as an important presence, is crucial. Look no further than Oscar Isaac. A compelling option and a beloved industry icon, Isaac excels at playing sharp, weary, morally complex survivors who carry deep internal trauma as excruciating baggage. Whether it be in Ex Machina, Dune, or Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens, his previous parts match the haunted resilience of a man eager to move on. He has a knack for playing characters who are cynical, quick-witted, and tired of the system, especially in the second season of Beef. Some fans may fear Isaac would be too put together for the part, but that's the beauty of acting! He can easily transform into the book-accurate Haymitch.

And now we begin our adventure into the colorful world of eccentric individuals! First up, the utterly fabulous Effie Trinket. The colorful, upbeat Capitol escort assigned to District 12 is deeply invested in Capitol etiquette, fashion, and rules, often appearing superficial or overly focused on decorum. Because of her rose-tinted glasses, she remains willfully oblivious to the harsh poverty beneath her in District 12. Though strictly focused on protocol, she slowly grows fond of the District 12 tributes. Elizabeth Banks brought her to life, grounding the over-the-top, satirical character with three-dimensional depth, humor, and heart. Banks crafted Effie's distinct theatricality and cadence by drawing inspiration from classic Hollywood icons.

Effie was infused with a relentless, chipper ebullience that made her feel like a real product of the Capitol's oppressive fascist society. She was a truly engaging character because there was always an alluring mystery tied to her. To capture the same exuberance with genuine heart that eventually seeps through, Alison Brie excels at playing tightly wound, rule-obsessed perfectionists who hide genuine vulnerability beneath a beautifully polished exterior. When it comes to rule-lovers who spiral when plans go off the rails, Brie's comedic precision shone as Annie Edison in Community. From there, she moved into the mix of camp and emotion during her run on GLOW. With a willingness to play modern satire through vocal agility, her voice-acting experience on BoJack Horseman would help her find the right tone for Effie's overtly affected inflection. Now, if you didn't think she could play big, bold, campy characters before, her recent turn as Evil-Lyn in Masters of the Universe is the perfect gateway to Effie Trinket's fabulosity. Put her in a towering wig and avant-garde wardrobe, and a new Effie is born.

No one was nearly as flamboyant, upbeat, and telegenic as the master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman. Serving as the primary media personality of the Capitol, his job is to put nervous tributes at ease, turn awkward interview moments into crowd-pleasing highlights, and make the brutal Hunger Games feel like an entertaining television spectacle. Caesar is known for his colorful, theatrical attire and annually dyeing his hair, lips, and eyelids in bright, changing themes. Dubbing Katniss as the infamous "Girl on Fire," Caesar was simply a hoot. Stanley Tucci blended smarmy insincerity, theatrical charisma, and subtle cruelty to satirize modern mass media and hypocrisy. Tucci styled Caesar with a glitzy, late-night talk show flair, radiating a fake, plastic warmth and faux sympathy while gleefully sending children off to slaughter.

Going full tilt with unnatural color and taped-back "face work," he exuded a shallow persona obsessed with entertainment as a means to distract from tyranny. Caesar must be played by an actor willing to go all-in in flamboyant theatricality. A phenomenal choice to play the seasoned version of the host is Sam Rockwell. Rockwell is infamous for his physical charisma, rhythmic delivery, and magnetic showmanship. Whether it's the wildly eccentric Zaphod Beeblebrox in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy or finding the humanity as Bob Fosse in Fosse/Verdon, Rockwell's innate theatricality would give him the range to make Caesar pop on the screen. His high-wattage energy, even in more grounded, realistic roles, is showcased by a smiling mask that covers a dark reality. In projects like Seven Psychopaths, Vice, and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, Rockwell has played characters whose charming, fast-talking exteriors hide moral compromise. Rockwell is naturally loose and unpredictable, which is essential for the improv-heavy Caesar. While he would give Caesar a darker edge than Tucci, Rockwell's versatility would translate, no matter what color his hair is.

Evil was personified in the form of President Coriolanus Snow. The tyrannical and ruthless ruler of the nation of Panem, the autocratic Snow maintains strict rule and control over the twelve districts through fear, propaganda, and the brutality of the Hunger Games. He is frequently associated with genetically modified white roses, which he uses to mask the odor of mouth sores caused by his history of poisoning rivals. With a cold, calculating demeanor, Donald Sutherland brought a chilling gravitas, deep political passion, and a quiet menace to a genuine monster in the first film and beyond. As a rationalizing, pragmatic villain, Sutherland portrayed Snow as a brilliant, dangerously calm authoritarian who genuinely believed his cold-blooded control and fear-based suppression was a necessary good. As a long-time activist, Sutherland wanted to ensure Snow was so tyrannical that it inspired political awareness and organization against systemic inequality. He succeeded.

Snow is anchored by chilling physical choices, namely his piercing gaze, soft-spoken smile, and calm acceptance of the physical toll of his past decisions. Sutherland had a natural villainy in his presence. An actor with that same innate evil imagery would be perfect to play President Snow in 2026. Very few actors exude evil with a simple glare quite like Willem Dafoe. His distinct physical features, intensity, and proven track record of playing layered, menacing, eccentric authority figures would let him find a new side of fear in Snow. He excels at playing men who are terrifying at first but deeply psychologically complex, like Norman Osborn in Spider-Man and Thomas Wake in The Lighthouse. His theatrical presence fits the dystopian tyrant archetype. Though Sutherland had a classical image, Dafoe's striking facial structure would convey aristocratic coldness and hidden cruelty without needing to say a word. Dafoe's Snow would be much darker, and isn't that just scary?

Behind every heroine is a personal stylist and costume designer who made them look like an icon. For Katniss, that visionary was Cinna. Assigned to create an image for the District 12 tributes, Cinna designed the dramatic, flame-engulfed opening-ceremony costumes for Katniss and Peeta that secured their vital corporate sponsor. Despite living a life of luxury in the Capitol, Cinna secretly took the assignment with District 12 to quietly align with the growing resistance against President Snow. Flamboyant in image and not in personality, Lenny Kravitz gave Cinna a calm, compassionate essence that was key to the character. As an accomplished musician and fashion-forward artist, Kravitz fit Cinna like a glove. He was naturally smooth with a self-assured poise.

Perhaps using Kravitz as the basis for casting, selecting another musician with fashion in the forefront would be sensational. It's time to feel the rush with Troye Sivan playing Cinna. Cinna is a visionary designer who stands out in the Capitol by rejecting garish excess in favor of sleek, intentional minimalism. Sivan's real-world presence as a fashion icon makes his authority as a couture mastermind completely believable. Cinna is a grounded individual, unlike the loud, theatrically eccentric citizens. Sivan has the gentleness that Cinna exudes, yet can also blend in with high-style charisma if needed. Sivan's artistic evolution, breaking away from commercial pop formulas for raw cultural impact, mirrors Cinna's willingness to risk everything to make a statement. A more contemporary, gender-fluid, and refined aesthetic would reflect how luxury fashion and rebellion look in 2026. Now, if you're wondering about his acting prowess, his resume ranges from X-Men Origins: Wolverine to The Idol.

Some of us dream of creating a brilliant game; Seneca Crane did just that. As the Head Gamemaker, Crane oversees the design and digital control of the survival arena. He orchestrated obstacles, environmental shifts, and hazards for the tributes. When Katniss and Peeta go rogue and threaten to commit suicide, Crane permits them both to survive. Seen as an act of dangerous defiance, Crane is executed. Though a minor, largely unseen background figure in the original novel, expanding him was a brilliant cinematic decision. Wes Bentley collaborated to give Crane his iconic aesthetic. The meticulously sculpted beard became a defining element of Crane. He created Crane in a manner that was an arrogant, out-of-touch showman who cared more about ratings and spectacle than human lives. And yet, when he does flip, it comes from a moment of ill-advised, reluctant sincerity.

Crane must have a quiet, eerie intensity that is defined by a calm, unbothered detachment that makes his sadistic game design feel even more chilling. With a resume filled with dark and twisted Ryan Murphy products, Joey Pollari could find that perfect balance of charm and evil. His ability to take on characters whose polished exteriors slowly crack under immense psychological pressure would translate into an enthralling take on Crane. Like Bentley, Pollari has an editorial, high-fashion edge that makes him a natural fit for the extravagant, image-obsessed elite of the Capitol. With a theater background alongside a resume of nuanced dramas like American Crime and Sugar, Pollari has the control and dramatic gravitas needed to sell the Gamemaker's control-room monologues as if he were directing live theater.

Last, but certainly not least, is Claudius Templesmith, the booming, resonant official announcer and commentator of the 74th Hunger Games. Serving alongside Caesar Flickerman, Claudius broke down and narrated the events for the Capitol audience. He broadcasts major official decrees to the tributes in the arena, including the start of the Games, inviting them to the Feast, changing the rules to allow two victors, and famously concluding his messages with the catchphrase, "May the odds be ever in your favor." Toby Jones brought a distinct, sharp comedic and theatrical energy to the role, capturing the chilling detachment of the Capitol's media machine. He played the part, almost emulating an American football broadcaster. When seen, he presented a physical, smiling, public-facing presence that mirrored how real-world media turns tragedy into spectacle.

While Jones had a specific brand of presentation, finding a performer with a booming presence to be the omniscient "Voice of the Capitol" requires someone who knows a thing or two about putting on a character voice. Look no further than Peter Serafinowicz. As a prolific voice actor, Serafinowicz has lent his talents to Darth Maul in The Phantom Menace and the Fisher King in Doctor Who. Possessing a rich, resonant baritone, he speaks and instantly commands authority. As an actor, whether it be the Sommelier in John Wick: Chapter 2 or Denarian Saal in Guardians of the Galaxy, he can effortlessly pivot from charming commentator to cold, sleek, and intimidating. He's known for mastering satirical news with a broadcast cadence on shows like Look Around You and The Peter Serafinowicz Show. He's perfected the overly polished, slightly detached cadence of a mid-century television presenter. With a blend of cheery professionalism and underlying absurdity, he would thrive as the Capitol's dystopian media machine. Now, if you need further proof that he can commentate on the fly, he's the absolute perfect fit as the humorous host of the reality social strategy series Million Dollar Secret. It's that same energy that would make Claudius astounding.

#3340. Apple Watch SE 3 vs Series 12: Which should you buy this holiday season?

The holiday shopping season is here, and Apple Watch is always a popular gift. Apple’s lineup includes the affordable Apple Watch SE 3 and the more advanced Apple Watch Series 12.

Here’s how those two Apple Watch models stack up…

The Apple Watch SE 3 is the most affordable way to enter the Apple Watch ecosystem. It got a big update last year, adding a variety of new higher-end Apple Watch features. It now offers an Always-On display, sleep apnea notifications, temperature sensing, interactive wrist flick and double tap gestures, and more.

The Apple Watch SE 3 offers 18 hours of battery life, though you can stretch that to 32 hours in Low Power Mode. It supports fast charging, going from 0-80% in 45 minutes.

Even though it hasn’t been updated in a year, the Apple Watch SE 3 is a very compelling option, especially for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem. It’s pretty fantastic that you can get an Apple Watch with key display and health-monitoring features for under $200.

The Apple Watch Series 12 is Apple’s newest smartwatch, and it’s a big update over its predecessor. This year, Apple doubled down on the health and fitness capabilities of Apple Watch with an all-new Health Sensing System.

Apple touts that the Apple Watch Series 12 delivers “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.” In fact, the company conducted a study of more than 1,000 participants that found the Series 12 “achieved statistically better overall accuracy than every competing wearable it tested across workouts and daily activities.”

With the new system, Apple Watch Series 12 captures your heart rate every five seconds. Previous Apple Watch models, including the Apple Watch SE 3, take measurements every five minutes. The new Health Sensing System also enables a new readiness score feature, which factors in your recent activity, training load, vitals, and sleep score.

As I wrote in my review, the Apple Watch Series 12 brings some of the biggest improvements to Apple Watch health tracking in years. The new sensing system unlocks a trove of new data along with better accuracy.

The Apple Watch lineup is incredibly strong right now. Whether you’re deciding between the SE 3 and Series 12, both offer great health tracking, battery life, and connectivity. The Apple Watch SE 3 is an excellent choice for people new to the Apple Watch ecosystem.

The Apple Watch Series 12, however, is the best Apple Watch for most people. There are major improvements to the health tracking capabilities, offering meaningful steps forward in what the Apple Watch can tell you about yourself. In the two months I’ve had mine, I’ve come to appreciate the more frequent heart rate measurement and readiness score.

What do you think of the current Apple Watch lineup? Are you shopping for one this holiday season? Let us know down in the comments.

#3338. Thanksgiving Earthquake Hits Off Baja California Coast, Magnitude 5.7

A magnitude 5.7 earthquake struck a remote group of islands off Mexico's Baja California peninsula on Thanksgiving ... delivering a holiday shake-up in the Pacific Ocean.

The quake hit Thursday near the Revillagigedo Islands, roughly 216 miles from Cabo San Lucas, at a depth of about 6 miles.

Fortunately, the remote location means the earthquake is unlikely to affect many people ... though it's unclear whether any aftershocks could strike closer to the mainland ... and the region was already rattled by a magnitude 4.2 earthquake just one day earlier.

The Revillagigedo Islands are volcanic and federally protected by Mexico, boasting such a rich marine ecosystem that National Geographic has dubbed them the "Galápagos of Mexico."

The Thanksgiving tremor comes just days after back-to-back earthquakes shook Southern California's beach cities ... including a magnitude 3.2 quake in Orange County early Monday and a magnitude 3.3 quake off Manhattan Beach on Sunday.

Mexico also experienced a magnitude 4.7 earthquake in Baja California earlier this month.

For now, it appears the holiday got off to a shaky start, with no major destruction.

#3337. Anthropic launches new Claude Ship feature for builders

Anthropic is launching a new tool for builders called Claude Ship. The new AI feature allows Claude to “review pull requests, fix them, and approve the ones that a team’s policy allows.”

Claude Ship is a new product created especially for builders who code with agents. The idea is to make handling pull requests as automated as agentic coding.

“That’s why we built Claude Ship, available today in beta,” Anthropic says. “It can review PRs, fix them, and decide what’s ready to merge based on policies each team sets. Teams stay in control of where it runs and which changes need a person. The goal: ship code as fast as teams write it.”

Claude Ship is comprised of three agents: Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals.

“Together, they take a pull request through review, fixes, and an approval decision so teams don’t have to manage each step manually,” Anthropic says.

“Developers can try Claude Ship on their own pull requests with the new /ship command in Claude Code,” Anthropic says.

You can learn much more about Claude Ship here. Additional documentation can be found here.
